findings.headline: Audit Wales review awarded council 'reasonable assurance with further improvement required' on recruitment and retention management
findings.detail: Audit Wales found council is taking positive actions including apprenticeship pathways, improved onboarding and increased HR capacity, but identified gaps in workforce intelligence, employee insight, corporate oversight and value-for-money assessment of interventions. The audit conclusion was qualified assurance indicating further improvement needed.
findings.matters: Finance directors care about governance and control effectiveness in operational areas affecting service delivery resilience
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: overall assurance assessment is reasonable assurance with further improvement required

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: Budget balance dependent on Welsh Government reimbursement described as "likely but far from wholly assured".
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget is "currently balanced only by relying on future likely (but far from wholly assured) reimbursement from Welsh Government, centrally held contingency budgets and reserves." This indicates the £13.678m overspend cannot be closed through operational management alone and requires external funding support that is uncertain.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders assess whether budget balance relies on own management actions or uncertain external sources. Dependence on unassured reimbursement signals budget sustainability risk.
findings.figures: £13.678m overspend dependent on unconfirmed Welsh Government reimbursement for closure
findings.quote: the budget overall is currently balanced only by relying on future likely (but far from wholly assured) reimbursement from Welsh Government, centrally held contingency budgets and reserves.

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: HRA responsive repairs underspend £3.15m available, though pressures in fire safety and grounds maintenance partially offset.
findings.detail: HRA responsive repairs budgeted at £13.65m is forecast to underspend by £3.15m to £10.5m based on current demand trends. However, cost pressures for fire door works (£190k) and grounds maintenance reductions (£525k) will partially offset this. Overall repairs and maintenance forecast £27.9m spend against £30.7m budget, an underspend of £2.8m.
findings.matters: HRA flexibility in repairs spending indicates demand moderation and provides headroom for reallocation to safety priorities.
findings.figures: Repairs budget £30.7m; forecast spend £27.9m; responsive repairs underspend £3.15m; fire doors pressure £190k; grounds maintenance pressure £525k
findings.quote: Based on current activity and projected demand, responsive repairs expenditure is forecast at £10.5m, resulting in an estimated underspend of £3.15m against budget.

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: Equal Pay provision of £28m likely to require material increase in-year, with deep earmarked reserve draws being considered for funding
findings.detail: The council holds £28m provision for Equal Pay claims. The S.151 Officer states it is "likely" to require material increase during the year. Funding options being evaluated include "deep use of existing earmarked reserves," signalling substantial exposure and risk of further reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Equal Pay is an unpredictable contingent liability for councils; material increases in provision erode available reserves and signal exposure to significant legacy pay gaps.
findings.figures: £28m existing Equal Pay provision; material increase anticipated in-year
findings.quote: There is also a significant ongoing risk around Equal Pay and it is likely that whilst there is an existing significant provision for this at £28m, this will need to be materially increased in year.

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: Contingency fund nearly fully allocated: £1.143m remaining of £11.894m opening balance.
findings.detail: Contingency Fund opened 2026/27 with £11.894m (£8.594m annual provision plus £3.3m brought forward from 2025/26). Current forecast calls total £10.751m, leaving £1.143m (9.6%) available for unplanned pressures. This narrow margin limits flexibility to respond to emerging risks.
findings.matters: Contingency reserves provide councils' buffer against demand volatility and unforeseen costs. A nearly committed contingency indicates limited headroom to manage in-year surprises.
findings.figures: £11.894m contingency opened; £10.751m allocated in forecast calls; £1.143m remaining unallocated
findings.quote: The Contingency Fund budgeted contribution was set at £8.594m contribution for 2026/27 as set out in the budget report approved by Council in March 2026. There was a balance brought forward from 2025/26 of £3.300m, so subject to final audit the total available for use in 2026/27 is £11.894m.

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: General Reserves already held below the S.151 Officer's minimum acceptable level.
findings.detail: The council's General Reserves are below the S.151 Officer's minimum threshold of acceptability. This limits financial resilience to absorb unexpected costs or volatility, and was noted before Q1 monitoring revealed the £13.678m overspend.
findings.matters: Low reserves signal vulnerability and indicate previous deficits have already consumed buffers. Lenders and peer councils watch reserve balances as early warning of financial stress.
findings.figures: General Reserves below minimum acceptable level (specific balance not disclosed in this excerpt)
findings.quote: it has low General Reserves already below the absolute minimum of acceptability to the S.151 Officer.

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: Pay award cost uncertainty: budget set at 2.5% but employers offer 3.3%, teachers award unresolved.
findings.detail: Revenue budget assumed 2.5% pay growth. The latest employers' offer is 3.3%, with £3.5m contingency provisionally allocated to cover the difference. Teachers' pay award is unresolved, with Welsh Government consulting on 3.5% plus uncertain partial grant funding. This creates cost risk dependent on external funding that may not cover the shortfall in future years.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable pay inflation erodes councils' ability to manage budgets. Unresolved awards with uncertain grant coverage signal budget planning risk.
findings.figures: 2.5% budget assumption vs 3.3% employers offer; 3.5% teachers consultation; £3.5m contingency set-aside for pay cost uplift
findings.quote: Given the significant uncertainty here it is far from clear what the final pay outcome or funding position (including longer term funding not just one off in year help) will be for teachers and schools.

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: Council Tax collection deficit forecast £2m in 2026/27, worsening from £1m deficit in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Council Tax income is forecast to produce a £2m deficit in 2026/27, a deterioration from the £1m deficit realised in 2025/26. This income weakness compounds the revenue overspend and must be covered from contingency and reserves.
findings.matters: Collection volatility is a material risk to councils' ability to fund services; peers and lenders monitor collection trends as early signals of economic stress in the local area.
findings.figures: £2m deficit forecast 2026/27; £1m deficit in 2025/26; doubling of deficit year-on-year
findings.quote: it is also (based on current trends) forecast that the level of Council Tax collection (which posted a deficit in 2025/26 of £1m) is likely to be a deficit in the region of £2m.

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: Social Services adult demand up 15%, driving £9.021m of £13.678m total overspend.
findings.detail: Adult Services is forecasting £9.021m overspend from 15% growth in new contacts and placements. Learning Disability residential care is up 12% (£2.6m overspend), supported living £2m overspend, mental health residential clients up 11% (£1.5m overspend), older people's domiciliary care £2.3m overspend. Child and Family Services adds £4.680m overspend from a shift to higher-cost residential placements.
findings.matters: Demand-led social care costs are a major budget risk across councils; the size and drivers of this growth signal whether local pressures are structural or temporary.
findings.figures: Adult Services £9.021m overspend; 15% demand growth; Learning Disability placements up 12%; Mental Health residential clients up 11%; Child & Family Services £4.680m overspend
findings.quote: Adult Services has experienced an estimated 15% average increase in demand, driven by significant growth in new contacts, residential placements, domiciliary care packages, supported living provision and the increasing volume of people requiring complex externally commissioned care

findings.paper_title: 12 (2 of 2) - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring 1st Quarter 202627
findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £13.678m forecast at Q1 2026/27, mainly from Social Services pressures.
findings.detail: The council forecast net directorate overspend of £13.678m at Q1. This is being mitigated by £1.143m contingency underspend and will require recovery through additional management actions and reserve draws. Savings are tracking at 97% of the £11.555m target (£11.249m achieved), but cost pressures from demand growth, inflation and pay awards exceed the base budget.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders assess how councils manage budget deficits and whether they rely on recurring management actions or one-off reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £13.678m overspend; £11.249m of £11.555m savings forecast achieved (97%); £1.143m contingency underspend forecast
findings.quote: This must be recovered by immediate widescale remedial action including significant spending restrictions.

findings.headline: Second temporary accommodation facility (Sun Alliance) scheduled to open February 2027
findings.detail: The Council's redesign includes a second facility at Boutique Student Living (Sun Alliance) in the city centre. At the time of the audit, this facility had not yet opened but was anticipated to become operational in February 2027, further expanding the Council's own provision.
findings.matters: Pipeline capital investment designed to further reduce reliance on expensive B&B accommodation; a lender would track progress on planned capital projects and their role in the cost control strategy
findings.figures: February 2027
findings.quote: The Council anticipates Sun Alliance becoming operational in February 2027.

findings.headline: Council has not clearly planned how to address limited move-on accommodation availability for temporary housing residents
findings.detail: The audit identifies a planning gap: the Council has not developed a clear plan to address limited availability of move-on (longer-term housing) accommodation. Without sufficient move-on options, people may remain in temporary accommodation longer than intended, potentially blocking the pathway and increasing risk of renewed reliance on expensive B&B accommodation.
findings.matters: A sustainability risk that could undermine the financial benefits of the Llys Glas investment if people cannot transition out of temporary accommodation, potentially driving costs back up
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Importantly, however, the Council has not clearly planned how it will address limited move-on options. The Council is aware that without sufficient move-on accommodation, people may stay in temporary accommodation longer than intended, blocking the pathway and increasing the risk of renewed reliance on B&B accommodation.

findings.headline: Council's arrangements to monitor overall value for money of temporary accommodation redesign are not yet fully developed
findings.detail: The audit finds that the Council has not established a comprehensive framework to assess the overall value for money of its redesign. While the Council monitors activity and reports cost avoidance from Llys Glas, it has not set out how it will measure outcomes and person-centred results over the medium to longer term.
findings.matters: A finance director would be concerned that a £7.2m annual service, plus capital investment, is being managed without clear outcome measures to demonstrate value for money and inform whether spending is delivering intended results
findings.figures: None specific to this gap
findings.quote: However, the Council's arrangements to monitor the overall value for money of its new approach are not yet fully developed. It intends to develop a wider set of person-centred outcome measures, including repeat presentations.

findings.headline: Council received average 80 homelessness presentations per week in 2025-26, peaking at 110, with predictions of exceeding 4,000 annually
findings.detail: The Council faces sustained and significant demand pressure for homelessness services. In 2025-26, it received an average of 80 presentations per week, with a peak of 110 in January 2026. The Council predicts that future annual presentations will exceed 4,000.
findings.matters: High and sustained demand is the underlying driver of costs and capital investment requirements; a finance director needs to understand demand trajectory to project future resource needs
findings.figures: 80 presentations per week average, peak of 110 in January 2026, future presentations to exceed 4,000 per year
findings.quote: In 2025-26, the Council received on average 80 homelessness presentations per week, with a peak of 110 in January. The Council predicts that future homelessness presentations will continue to exceed 4,000 per year.

findings.headline: Llys Glas temporary accommodation facility opened in April 2026 and reduced B&B placements to 283 from 341 by end-March
findings.detail: The Council's capital investment in its own temporary accommodation facility is showing early results. Following the opening of Llys Glas (developed with Pobl and Welsh Government support), the number of households in B&B accommodation fell significantly, from 341 to 283 by the end of March 2026.
findings.matters: Capital investment designed to reduce revenue costs; a finance director would track whether capital projects deliver intended savings and identify early evidence of impact
findings.figures: B&B households fell from 341 to 283; total temporary accommodation fell from 419 to 389
findings.quote: The number of households in B&B fell to 283 by the end of March 2026 following the opening of Llys Glas (the Council's temporary accommodation scheme developed with Pobl and Welsh Government).

findings.headline: B&B accommodation expenditure increased from £6 million in 2024-25 to £7.2 million in 2025-26
findings.detail: The Council faces rising costs in temporary accommodation provision. B&B accommodation, which is more expensive than planned alternatives, increased year-on-year by £1.2 million. This cost growth is the immediate driver behind the Council's decision to redesign its approach and develop its own facilities.
findings.matters: A material annual cost that is growing year-on-year; a finance director at this or another council would need to track whether cost control measures are working
findings.figures: £6 million in 2024-25, £7.2 million in 2025-26
findings.quote: The Council's gross spend on B&B accommodation increased from £6 million in 2024/25 to £7.2 million in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 07 (2 of 2) - Published Strategic Risk and Issues Q1 2026-27 - 6 July 2026 Open
findings.headline: Homelessness and housing supply demand sustained at high level; sector delivery cannot meet identified need
findings.detail: The council faces sustained high demand for homelessness support and social housing that housing sector delivery programmes cannot meet. The issue score has remained at 16 throughout the 12-month period. While control measures are in place (development partners, new unit tenders, RSL partnerships), they do not indicate resolution of the underlying demand-supply mismatch.
findings.matters: Sustained housing shortfalls create ongoing pressure on temporary accommodation costs (already bridge-funded unsustainably from General Fund) and constrain Regeneration Programme housing delivery targets.
findings.figures: Homelessness and housing issue score 16 throughout July 2025-June 2026; no improvement
findings.quote: The increasing number of homelessness presentations and growing demand for social housing is putting pressure on housing, tenancy support and other Council services as well as increasing costs.

findings.paper_title: 07 (2 of 2) - Published Strategic Risk and Issues Q1 2026-27 - 6 July 2026 Open
findings.headline: Supply chain volatility risk raised; geopolitical disruption spreading beyond energy into most council services
findings.detail: The council has raised its supply chain volatility risk assessment from 9 to 12, reflecting that geopolitical disruption is no longer confined to energy and gas but affecting most council operations and services. Risk appetite is Averse, meaning any further increase must be reported immediately.
findings.matters: Supply chain disruption increases project delivery delays and cost inflation across capital and revenue programmes; councils must build contingencies into programme and budget estimates.
findings.figures: Supply chain volatility risk raised to 12 (from 9); risk appetite Averse
findings.quote: risk raised given ongoing geopolitical risks and emerging secondary wave effects beyond oil/gas into most other services

findings.paper_title: 07 (2 of 2) - Published Strategic Risk and Issues Q1 2026-27 - 6 July 2026 Open
findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grants 2026-27 budget fully committed by pipeline schemes, with waiting lists growing following removal of means-testing
findings.detail: Demand for DFG adaptations has exceeded service capacity following removal of means-testing. Waiting lists have grown significantly, with unacceptable delays for disabled residents. The capital programme budget is explicitly identified as at risk of running out. The latest comment confirms 2026-27 demand remains high with significant pipeline commitments already exhausting the year's budget.
findings.matters: DFG budget depletion would force cuts to a statutory service, delay support to vulnerable residents, and create additional pressure on social care and health services.
findings.figures: Issue score 16 throughout; 2026-27 budget already fully committed by pipeline schemes
findings.quote: The DFG capital programme could run out the funds in future years if mitigating actions are not put in place.

findings.paper_title: 07 (2 of 2) - Published Strategic Risk and Issues Q1 2026-27 - 6 July 2026 Open
findings.headline: Welsh Government temporary accommodation funding does not meet demand; General Fund bridging shortfall throughout July 2025-June 2026
findings.detail: WG funding for temporary accommodation does not meet actual demand. The council is bridge-funding the shortfall from its General Fund, which it describes as unsustainable. The issue score has remained at 16 (high) throughout the entire 12-month period, indicating chronic rather than transient pressure.
findings.matters: Service-specific grant shortfalls that transfer to General Fund create ongoing revenue pressure; described as unsustainable, signalling either future service cuts or reallocation from other budgets.
findings.figures: Issue score 16 throughout July 2025-June 2026; no improvement recorded
findings.quote: Currently the level of funding is insufficient given the high numbers, and the General Fund is having to meet the shortfall which is not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: 07 (2 of 2) - Published Strategic Risk and Issues Q1 2026-27 - 6 July 2026 Open
findings.headline: HRA unable to identify significant additional financial resources including Welsh Government funding
findings.detail: Swansea's Housing Revenue Account cannot identify sufficient additional funding to deliver its More Homes Strategy targets or meet Welsh Housing Quality Standard compliance. The risk score has remained at 12 throughout the period. Control measures focus on lobbying Welsh Government and pursuing external grants but do not address the structural funding gap.
findings.matters: HRA funding shortfalls constrain new housing delivery and maintenance, driving spillover pressure into General Fund services (temporary accommodation, homelessness support) and limiting Regeneration Programme progress.
findings.figures: HRA risk score 12 throughout July 2025-June 2026; target score 4; no improvement trend
findings.quote: The Authority is unable to identify significant additional HRA financial resources, including WG funding and therefore will not be able to fully achieve key strategic and political objectives such as targets set under the More Homes Strategy and meet its statutory obligations to maintain the Welsh Housing Quality Standard.

findings.paper_title: 07 (2 of 2) - Published Strategic Risk and Issues Q1 2026-27 - 6 July 2026 Open
findings.headline: Budget overspend risk peaked at maximum level in February-March 2026 due to outturn, unfunded pressures, and one-off cost events
findings.detail: The risk score for living within the annual budget spiked to 25 (the highest possible) in February-March 2026, driven by outturn pressures, unfunded cost increases, pay and inflation, and identified one-off cost events. The score has since recovered to 8 by June 2026. The target score is 9, indicating ongoing concern. This spike reflects real budget control pressures that the council managed within the financial year.
findings.matters: Budget overspends require reserve depletion, reducing resilience; sustained unfunded pressures indicate Welsh Government funding does not cover actual service costs.
findings.figures: Risk score peaked at 25 in February-March 2026 (equal to inherent score); recovered to 8 by June 2026; target score 9
findings.quote: Impact significantly raised upwards given outturn, unfunded pressures, pay and inflation and looming one off significant cost events

findings.headline: Senior leaders do not have timely access to recruitment and retention data in a usable format, limiting oversight of the council's largest cost area.
findings.detail: The council collects recruitment and retention data and reports some metrics quarterly to Corporate Management Team, but extracting the data is described as labour-intensive and not readily available for officers to understand specific challenges. A dashboard to improve this is under development but not yet operational. This means senior leaders cannot easily monitor spending and performance in the cost area that constitutes the majority of the budget.
findings.matters: Weak real-time visibility of spending and performance in the largest cost area creates risk of unidentified overspends, ineffective resource allocation, or delayed responses to emerging problems. A lender would see this as a control weakness in financial management.
findings.figures: Some data, such as the time taken to recruit, is reported quarterly to Corporate Management Team
findings.quote: However, senior leaders do not always have timely access to the data they need, in a suitable format. We were told that extracting the data is a labour-intensive process. The Council has plans to develop a dashboard to address this issue, but this is still under development.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges that historic budget cuts to central Human Resources capacity impaired its ability to understand and manage recruitment and retention challenges, now taking steps to rebuild this.
findings.detail: The council recognises that past decisions to cut HR central services weakened its management capability in an area that is critical during times of budget pressure. It is now actively increasing HR capacity specifically for recruitment and retention activity, indicating awareness that this previous cut created a gap in financial and workforce management.
findings.matters: Shows how past cost-reduction decisions can weaken a council's operational management of its largest cost base, potentially making current budget pressures harder to manage. A finance director at another council would note this as a cautionary example about the long-term cost of capacity cuts.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Council understands that historic decisions to make budget cuts to central services have impaired its ability to understand and manage its recruitment and retention challenges. The Council is taking steps to increase its Human Resources (HR) capacity, to manage recruitment processes more effectively and to prepare for longer-term challenges.

findings.headline: Council does not assess or monitor the value for money of its recruitment and retention approaches, despite workforce comprising the majority of day-to-day spending.
findings.detail: The council spends most of its budget on workforce costs (stated in paragraph 3) and uses various approaches including fixed-term contracts, external agency staff, and market supplements to manage recruitment and retention. One documented example shows that restructuring Legal Services to speed recruitment reduced outsourced legal work and saved money, but the council has not evaluated this financial impact and has no corporate oversight of which approaches represent better value for money.
findings.matters: Workforce is typically a council's largest cost area. Without systematic value-for-money assessment, a council may be missing efficiency opportunities, overspending on temporary solutions like agency staff, or failing to identify where a given approach is cost-effective.
findings.figures: Majority of the Council's day-to-day spending is used to pay for its workforce; Council has reduced reliance on agency workers in its waste service, having identified benefits of creating permanent positions
findings.quote: The Council does not assess or monitor the value for money of its approach to recruitment and retention. There are examples where a change to its recruitment approach has led to reduced costs or improved the service. For example, the Council recognised that the protracted recruitment process in Legal Services was inefficient, so provided more resources to speed this up. In doing so, the service benefitted from increased recruitment and retention levels, which reduced the amount of outsourced legal work and saved the Council money. But the Council has not evaluated the financial impact of this change and there is no corporate or strategic oversight of which approaches represent better value for money.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer reports all directorates likely to find it "increasingly hard to live within budgets" due to inflation and social care demand
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer states it is 'likely that all Directorates will find it increasingly hard to live within budgets primarily due to both inflationary and demand pressures on services, predominantly in social care.' This describes current dynamics, not future risk, indicating budget management pressures are acute in 2026/27 and may worsen.
findings.matters: If all directorates are currently struggling with budgets, there is significant risk of in-year overspend and uncontrolled use of reserves in the current financial year. This suggests the medium-term deficit forecast may be optimistic about the council's ability to hold spending.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: Equally, it is likely that all Directorates will find it increasingly hard to live within budgets primarily due to both inflationary and demand pressures on services, predominantly in social care.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges need for major structural service change with significant costs and employment impact, but transformation plan and financing remain uncertain.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer reports that the council must 'prepare for significant change in service delivery that will inevitably impact on direct employment levels going forward' and identifies this as 'a significant financial risk given the scale and pace of budget pressures'. The officer notes transformation will require 'substantial up-front costs' and investment in digital technology, but the detailed plan and change costs are still being worked through.
findings.matters: Structural change is the mechanism for delivering the £54.8m+ of required savings, but the council has not yet finalised its transformation plan or change costs, adding execution risk to the deficit recovery strategy.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: It is the opinion of the Section 151 Officer that the Council needs to continue to prepare for significant change in service delivery that will inevitably impact on direct employment levels going forward.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan forecasts £54.8m cumulative deficit by 2029/30, with the council expecting this will worsen due to equal pay costs.
findings.detail: The MTFP approved in March 2026 forecast a cumulative deficit of £54.8m by end of 2029/30, based on assumption of 2% annual government funding growth. Savings targets are £12.7m for 2026/27 and £8.3m for 2027/28. However, the Section 151 Officer warns that equal pay costs will push the deficit larger, because the council will need to both repay reserves it has drawn down and any alternative sources of financing will be costly and reduce resources elsewhere.
findings.matters: The published deficit forecast is material and conservative (assumes continued government funding growth). The officer's warning that equal pay will worsen the position suggests the council's current financial plan is incomplete and the deficit recovery task will be larger than the headline figure.
findings.figures: £54.8m cumulative deficit by 2029/30; savings requirement £12.7m (2026/27) plus £8.3m (2027/28)
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Plan approved by Council on 5th March 2026 forecast a cumulative deficit on General Fund Revenue Expenditure of some £54.8m by 2029/30

findings.headline: £22.3m of earmarked reserves are being reclassified to fund equal pay, but only £4.1m is permanent; £18.8m must be rebuilt.
findings.detail: The council is reducing earmarked reserves from £82.8m to £60.5m through reclassification. Of the £22.3m reduction, approximately £4.1m is considered permanently available for equal pay, while £18.8m consists of maintenance and equipment renewal reserves that must be replenished over time. The Section 151 Officer explicitly identifies the risk: if renewal needs materialise before reserves are rebuilt, the authority may be forced to use expensive external borrowing to replace worn-out assets.
findings.matters: The reserve draw is temporary rather than structural, betting that spending can be deferred while reserves are rebuilt. The council's own officer has flagged that this plan is risky; if renewal needs materialise before reserves are rebuilt, the authority faces unplanned borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves reducing from £82,801k to £60,487k (reduction of £22,314k); of reclassified reserves £4.1m permanent, £18.8m temporary
findings.quote: The overriding risk will be that the replacement of the reserve won't be achieved before the purpose of the reserve becomes an imperative expenditure item.

findings.headline: General reserve of £10m is now below the council's certified minimum level for financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The general reserve was budgeted at £14m in March 2026. Following the £4m transfer to equal pay provisions in July, it now stands at £10m. The council has formally stated this is below the minimum level it certified as adequate for an authority of its size. The Section 151 Officer notes the council is 'holding a very low level of General Reserve for the size of the authority'.
findings.matters: General reserve is the council's contingency for unexpected events and budget smoothing. Being below the certified minimum level directly indicates reduced financial resilience and capacity to absorb further shocks.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance £10,000k; reduced from £14m budgeted in March 2026
findings.quote: It is now temporarily below the certified minimum level as set out in budget setting for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Equal pay settlement cost remains unresolved but material, forcing immediate reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: In July 2026, the council transferred £4m from general reserve to increase the equal pay provision after the original budget assumption proved inadequate. Since then, the provision has been assessed as still insufficient. The final cost will be significant but remains unresolved due to ongoing litigation and negotiation. The council will need to implement 'several major sources of financing' to address this within the financial year.
findings.matters: An unresolved but acknowledged material liability creates both immediate cash pressure and uncertainty about future costs, forcing the council to raid general reserves and raising questions about whether other funding sources including borrowing will be required.
findings.figures: £4m transferred from general reserve to equal pay in July 2026; General reserve now £10,000k
findings.quote: Since 31st March 2026 it has become clearer that the provision set aside for Equal Pay will need to be further increased by a material amount, though the total scale remains unresolved given parallel litigation and negotiation.

findings.headline: The education capital programme has a £73.571m adverse variance pending a Welsh Government cost standard review
findings.detail: The education capital programme is subject to a Welsh Government cost standard review. The variance reported of £73.571m represents 'the current cost estimate of the original proposed budgeted projects.' The paper states this 'will simply lead to a reprioritisation of the planned schools programme to meet the affordability of the schools programme (circa £400m of which the Council is funding £100m).' A quarter-two update is promised but the scale of the pressure is unclear.
findings.matters: A £73.571m education capital programme variance that will force reprioritisation signals that the council's school building ambitions cannot be afforded at current cost levels, and delivery will need to be scaled back.
findings.figures: £73.571m adverse variance in Education capital; original programme ~£400m with Council funding ~£100m
findings.quote: The Education Capital programme is currently subject to a schools projects cost review using the Welsh Governments revised cost standard. The variance to the end of the programme of £73.571m simply represents the current cost estimate of the original proposed budgeted projects. This does not mean that there is a financial pressure as this will simply lead to a reprioritisation of the planned schools programme to meet the affordability of the schools programme (circa £400m of which the Council is funding £100m).

findings.headline: Equal Pay provision of £28m is forecast to be 'materially increased in year' with no identified funding source
findings.detail: The council notes 'There is also a significant ongoing risk around Equal Pay and it is likely that whilst there is an existing significant provision for this at £28m, this will need to be materially increased in year. There are a number of options being considered to fund this including deep use of existing earmarked reserves and several potential capital flexibilities that will likely be brought to Council in October and November.' This is an unquantified contingent liability.
findings.matters: An unquantified increase to a £28m provision suggests exposure beyond current visibility, and the fact that funding is not yet identified means it will be covered by further reserve drawdown or capital flexibility moves that reduce flexibility elsewhere.
findings.figures: £28m existing Equal Pay provision; increase needed in-year, amount unspecified
findings.quote: There is also a significant ongoing risk around Equal Pay and it is likely that whilst there is an existing significant provision for this at £28m, this will need to be materially increased in year. There are a number of options being considered to fund this including deep use of existing earmarked reserves and several potential capital flexibilities

findings.headline: Savings achievement is only 97%, and requires £3.835m 'temporary mitigation' to reach even that level
findings.detail: Against a £11.555m savings target, the council forecasts £11.249m (97%) will be achieved. Of that £11.249m, £3.835m requires 'Temporary Mitigation to Achieve Target' — it is not sustainable delivery of the savings plan but short-term fixing. This means permanent structural savings are only £7.414m against a target of £11.555m.
findings.matters: If 33% of forecast savings delivery depends on one-time mitigation rather than permanent measures, the council will face a larger deficit in 2027/28 when those mitigations expire.
findings.figures: £11.555m savings target; £11.249m forecast achieved (97%); £3.835m requires temporary mitigation
findings.quote: A summary of this progress is attached at Appendix C... shows that against a savings target of £11.555m, £11.249m or some 97% is forecast to be achieved by the end of the year.

findings.headline: General reserves are already below the S.151 officer's minimum acceptable threshold
findings.detail: The S.151 officer explicitly states in paragraph 5 that the council 'has low General Reserves already below the absolute minimum of acceptability to the S.151 Officer.' This is stated as a baseline risk before the year's pressures emerge.
findings.matters: Inadequate general reserves leave the council with no buffer for unplanned spending and severely limit financial flexibility.
findings.figures: General reserves below minimum acceptable level (specific amount not disclosed)
findings.quote: it has low General Reserves already below the absolute minimum of acceptability to the S.151 Officer

findings.headline: Council Tax collection has deteriorated: £2m deficit forecast in 2026/27, up from £1m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a Council Tax collection deficit of £2m against the budget. This follows a £1m deficit in 2025/26. This is not a timing issue but a structural shortfall in income. The deficit is being made up by drawing down the general fund.
findings.matters: Deteriorating council tax collection is a signal of household stress and signals that the council's income base is contracting, not a temporary blip.
findings.figures: £2m Council Tax collection deficit forecast 2026/27; £1m deficit in 2025/26
findings.quote: forecast that the level of Council Tax collection (which posted a deficit in 2025/26 of £1m) is likely to be a deficit in the region of £2m

findings.headline: Pay inflation (3.3% vs 2.5% budgeted) creates £3.5m unbudgeted pressure, and teachers' pay award is still unresolved
findings.detail: Service variations assume 2.5% pay award but the latest employers' offer is 3.3%, creating £3.5m pressure being held in contingency. Teachers' pay is more acute: the Welsh Government is consulting on a 3.5% offer with only partial grant funding. The council states 'it is far from clear what the final pay outcome or funding position (including longer term funding not just one off in year help) will be for teachers and schools.' This £3.5m contingency allocation cannot be used elsewhere.
findings.matters: Pay inflation cannot be controlled by the council and £3.5m of contingency is already earmarked for it before the year has started, with the full exposure still unknown.
findings.figures: £3.5m pay award pressure in contingency; 3.3% actual offer vs 2.5% budgeted; teachers' pay settled on Welsh Government consultation at 3.5% with partial funding only
findings.quote: The latest employers offer is 3.3%. The anticipated increase has been set aside from Contingency. A teachers pay offer recommendation has been made for Wales by the independent remuneration board, but Welsh Ministers are consulting on a lower 3.5% offer with a potential grant funding offer to Councils to partially fund the still higher than expected award in year. Given the significant uncertainty here it is far from clear what the final pay outcome or funding position (including longer term funding not just one of in year help) will be for teachers and schools.

findings.headline: Adult social care demand surged 15%, driving £13.603m of the total £13.678m overspend
findings.detail: Social Services is forecasting £13.603m overspend, with the Director reporting 'estimated 15% average increase in demand, driven by significant growth in new contacts, residential placements, domiciliary care packages, supported living provision.' Within Adult Services alone, Learning Disability residential placements are overspending by £2.6m and supported living by £2m, with Mental Health residential up £1.5m and Older People's Domiciliary Care up £2.3m. Child and Family Services adds £4.68m driven by a shift to higher-cost external residential placements.
findings.matters: A 15% surge in demand for social care is not a one-year event and signals the council cannot predict or control its largest single cost driver. The overspend is demand-led, not process failure, which means it will recur.
findings.figures: £13.603m Social Services overspend; 15% demand growth; £2.6m Learning Disability residential; £2m Supported Living; £1.5m Mental Health residential; £2.3m Older People's Domiciliary Care
findings.quote: Adult Services has experienced an estimated 15% average increase in demand, driven by significant growth in new contacts, residential placements, domiciliary care packages, supported living provision and the increasing volume of people requiring complex externally commissioned care

findings.headline: A £13.678m revenue deficit is being covered by reserve drawdown, not current spending control
findings.detail: Net service expenditure is forecast to overspend by £13.678m. The council is 'currently balanced only by relying on future likely (but far from wholly assured) reimbursement from Welsh Government, centrally held contingency budgets and reserves.' The S.151 officer forecasts it 'looks inevitable as this early stage that material draws from contingency and some earmarked reserves will be needed to achieve a fully balanced budget for the year.' Only £1.143m contingency underspend is forecast to remain.
findings.matters: A council covering a structural deficit with one-time reserve draws cannot sustain this into future years, and signals underlying spending pressures it cannot control.
findings.figures: £13.678m overspend; £11.894m total contingency available; £1.143m forecast underspend at year end
findings.quote: the budget overall is currently balanced only by relying on future likely (but far from wholly assured) reimbursement from Welsh Government, centrally held contingency budgets and reserves

findings.headline: Most fraud control improvements will not be implemented until March-May 2027
findings.detail: The council has agreed to all nine recommendations and produced a management action plan. However, only one action (pre-employment checks review) is scheduled for completion by December 2026. Five actions have March 2027 implementation dates and three have May 2027 dates, meaning control gaps will persist for 5-9 months.
findings.matters: Delays in closing audit-identified control gaps extend the period during which fraud detection capacity remains below auditor recommendations
findings.figures: December 2026: 1 action; March 2027: 5 actions; May 2027: 3 actions
findings.quote: The Council's response to the nine recommendations made can be found in the Management Action Plan in Appendix 1.

findings.headline: Audit Wales found the council lacks a comprehensive fraud risk assessment and counter fraud delivery plan
findings.detail: While Audit Wales gave a positive overall message, the auditors identified specific gaps: the absence of a comprehensive fraud risk assessment and a counter fraud delivery plan. They also noted opportunities to strengthen pre-employment checks, intelligence sharing, and publicising detected fraud.
findings.matters: Weak fraud detection frameworks could allow financial irregularities to go undetected, and auditor findings on control adequacy inform lender confidence in the council's governance and financial reporting reliability
findings.figures: 9 recommendations for improvement; 1 existing positive finding from previous 2020 Auditor General report
findings.quote: The report also noted that Audit Wales believe that there are some improvements that can be made with current arrangements. The report noted that these include the absence of a comprehensive fraud risk assessment and a counter fraud delivery plan.

findings.headline: Significant capital condition surveys of major council buildings will drive MTFP commitments.
findings.detail: The Council has commissioned a comprehensive rolling condition survey of 112 council assets (including the Guildhall, Civic Centre, and Grand Theatre). A desktop assessment of the Guildhall has been completed and shared with CEO/Director to inform capital MTFP; officers have been commissioned to assess the Civic Centre and Grand Theatre. Findings will be reported to CMT by December 2026 with recommendations on how to embed the work into the Asset Management Plan and capital processes.
findings.matters: Large deferred maintenance backlogs can force sudden, unplanned capital spending that squeezes other priorities. This systematic assessment may reveal how much the Council needs to commit to building maintenance.
findings.figures: 112 assets surveyed; rolling 5-year update cycle planned; specific defects and costs to be determined
findings.quote: A thorough desk top assessment has been produced for the Guildhall and shared with the CEO / Director. This will inform the capital MTFP. Officers have been commissioned to complete assessments on the Civic Centre and Grand Theatre.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs require ongoing mitigation as transition from B&B to supported housing continues.
findings.detail: The Council opened Llys Glas (supported housing facility) in December 2025 and is developing a second scheme for late 2026/27. A Housing Support Grant procurement exercise is underway to increase fixed-site capacity. However, the tracker notes "the lack of affordable housing and the numbers presenting as homeless continues to provide barriers" to achieving objectives. Housing Options staff continue to use B&B where necessary, and a separate Audit Wales individual audit examined the Council's value-for-money in temporary accommodation provision.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a growing cost pressure for councils. B&B placements are expensive and inflexible. A lender needs to understand whether the Council's transition strategy will reduce costs or if demand will outpace supply.
findings.figures: Llys Glas opened December 2025; second scheme anticipated late 2026-27; specific placement numbers or costs not in this tracker
findings.quote: Following on from their all Wales audit, Audit Wales are currently carrying out an individual audit and will be looking out how Swansea are making the transition from Bed & Breakfast into more suitable forms of temporary accommodation. Llys Glas is now fully operational

findings.headline: Building Control faces recruitment delays implementing new statutory obligations.
findings.detail: The Council is recruiting to meet Building Safety Act requirements but is behind schedule. An LABC apprentice was appointed after the previous one finished in December 2025, and recruitment for a Senior Building Control Officer is ongoing. Operational Standard Rules from Welsh Government have not yet been released, creating uncertainty about service design.
findings.matters: Building Control is typically a fee-earning service that should recover costs. Understaffing and statutory implementation delays risk service failures and regulatory breaches that could trigger intervention.
findings.figures: LABC apprentice appointed December 2025; new apprentice started January 2026; Senior officer recruitment in progress
findings.quote: We have confirmed to appoint our current LABC apprentice when he finishes his apprenticeship in December 2025, this will increase our number of surveyors. We have also confirmed that we will be taking on a new LABC apprentice in January 2026 for the 2 year cycle. We are also looking at recruitment options for a Senior Building Control Officer.

findings.headline: Savings delivery requires stronger mitigations to offset shortfalls against original plans.
findings.detail: The Council's new savings reporting tracker distinguishes business-as-usual from transformation savings, but multiple quarterly updates note that "mitigations being significantly beefed up to provide more rounded track of savings and equivalence/action to offset if short on original plan." This indicates actual savings are not matching the Council's original plans and compensating actions are needed.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether planned budget savings will materialize. Evidence that savings are repeatedly short and require substitution suggests unreliability in the savings programme.
findings.figures: Savings tracked quarterly via reporting tracker; specific shortfalls not quantified in this document
findings.quote: Reporting tracker has been amended for formal reports. Outturn being completed during May/June 2026 for Cabinet July 2026. Mitigations being significantly beefed up to provide more rounded track of savings and equivalence/action to offset if short on original plan.

findings.headline: Committee effectiveness score (82.44%) is notably lower than governance and membership scores, with uncertainty about whether the committee evaluates and acts on its own weaknesses.
findings.detail: The effectiveness section scores 82.44% versus 91%+ in other sections. Key weaknesses include: only 3 of 9 members confident the committee evaluates whether it adds value (Q27), and member collaboration on this self-assessment itself lacks consensus with 1 member marking non-compliance (Q29). An action plan to address weakness is questioned by 1 member marking significant improvement needed (Q28).
findings.matters: A finance director needs to trust the audit committee to drive improvement. Lower effectiveness scores and internal disagreement on improvement planning suggest the committee may struggle to address control weaknesses it identifies.
findings.figures: Effectiveness category score 82.44%, Question 27 (value evaluation) 3 (33.3%) fully complies, Question 28 (action plan) 1 (11.1%) significantly complies, Question 29 (collaborative assessment) 1 (11.1%) does not comply
findings.quote: Has the committee evaluated whether and how it is adding value to the organisation?

findings.headline: Audit committee has not consistently met privately with external auditors and internal audit head, a governance gap flagged by 6 of 9 committee members.
findings.detail: Question 12 asks whether the committee met privately with external auditors and head of internal audit in the last year. Only 3 of 9 committee members say this is fully complied with. Two members report it does not comply, and four indicate it requires minor improvement. Private meetings with auditors are essential to enable unfiltered discussion of audit concerns and audit independence.
findings.matters: A lender depends on the audit committee as a control mechanism. If the committee is not meeting privately with auditors, it cannot effectively challenge management or receive candid audit feedback. This is a control weakness.
findings.figures: Question 12: 2 (22.2%) Does not comply, 4 (44.4%) Minor improvement, 3 (33.3%) No further improvement
findings.quote: Has the committee met privately with the external auditors and head of internal audit in the last year?

findings.headline: Over 150 restricted grants annually with inconsistent design, monitoring, and administration requirements
findings.detail: Welsh Government grant processes lack consistent quality assurance. Individual grants vary widely in their conditions, monitoring requirements, and administrative demands. The Grant Assurance Panel reviews proposals but its recommendations are advisory, not mandatory. A senior council finance officer may need to approve 1,000+ grant documents annually. Some low-value grants (£178 examples cited) require complex administration.
findings.matters: High administrative burden of managing many inconsistent grants diverts council finance resources from strategic work. This increases council costs and can distract from proactive financial planning. A lender should consider this as part of understanding council finance team capacity and quality.
findings.figures: Over 150 restricted grants to councils annually; senior CFOs approve 1,000+ grant documents annually; example of £178 in-year grant addition requiring processing
findings.quote: One senior council finance officer estimated they approve over 1,000 restricted grant documents each year. This can include, for example, submitting claim forms even when a council is not claiming any money (known as a nil claim).

findings.headline: Welsh Government has no protocol for supporting councils that issue section 114 (cannot balance budget) reports
findings.detail: No section 114 reports have been made in Welsh councils. When asked about support if one were issued, councils reported unclear understanding of what the Welsh Government would do. Some councils mistakenly believe a section 114 report would trigger additional funding, though the Welsh Government is clear it would not. The Welsh Government is drafting a protocol but has not finalised it.
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial sustainability risk needs to understand that if a Welsh council does get into severe financial difficulty (unable to balance budget), there is no published framework for intervention or support. This affects the lender's understanding of worst-case escalation.
findings.figures: No section 114 reports made in Wales to date; draft protocol in development but not finalised
findings.quote: Not being clear on what would happen after a section 114 report is made can have a negative impact on financial decision-making. For example, during our interviews we heard there is a misconception amongst some members and officers that issuing a section 114 report will lead to the Welsh Government providing more funding.

findings.headline: 28% of funding allocation data is from 2001 or earlier; Standard Spending Assessment formula last independently reviewed in 2002
findings.detail: The SSA formula allocates £1.4 billion (17% of total settlement) based on data at least 9 years old, including 1991 census data and 2001 census data. Data from 1991 is used for settlement size; 2001 data for pensioners and children in lone households. This outdated data may misallocate funding between councils.
findings.matters: If a council's funding is calculated on data that no longer reflects its demographics or needs, it may be underfunded or overfunded relative to actual service demand. This affects both the council's budgeting accuracy and the lender's view of its structural position.
findings.figures: £1.4 billion allocated based on data from 1991, 2001, or 2017; 72% of data is from 2023 or later; 17% is from 2001; 5% from 1991
findings.quote: 17% – The share of the IBAs allocated on the basis of data indicators in the 2025-26 settlement calculated using data from 1991 or 2001. This equates to £1.4 billion.

findings.headline: Welsh Government allocates 20% of annual restricted grant funding (£1.5 billion in March 2025) in the final month of the financial year
findings.detail: Grants are announced at separate times throughout the year; in 2024-25, one-fifth of total restricted grant funding was allocated in March alone. Some councils receive grants with only 7-25 days to spend them, creating pressure for short-term or opportunistic spending decisions.
findings.matters: Late allocation of large sums forces councils into rushed procurement and spending that may not represent value for money, and makes forecasting cash flow and outcomes difficult. Example: Sustainable Waste Management Grant (£16.4m) was not confirmed until nine months into 2025-26.
findings.figures: £1.5 billion (20% of annual total) allocated in March 2025; councils given 7-25 days in some cases to spend grants; Sustainable Waste Management Grant (£16.4m) not confirmed until month nine
findings.quote: Councils shared examples where they had been given between seven and 25 days to spend the grant. This significantly increases the risk of short-term decisions that deliver poor value for money.

findings.headline: Welsh Government gives councils less than two months to set budgets after announcing the settlement
findings.detail: The settlement announcement has moved from October/December (pre-pandemic) to December/February. Councils must set Council Tax and balanced budgets by 11 March each year. This compressed timeline increases pressure on officers and reduces time for public consultation on budget proposals.
findings.matters: A lender assessing a Welsh council's financial resilience needs to understand that budget-setting is rushed and may not reflect full scrutiny of spending plans, particularly affecting medium-term capital planning.
findings.figures: Settlement timing moved from October/December to December/February since 2020-21; councils have roughly 6 weeks between final settlement and 11 March budget deadline
findings.quote: The reduced time for councils to set their revenue budgets following the settlement can have impacts on how they plan their capital spending.

findings.paper_title: 06 (3 of 3) - Appendix 2 AW Swansea Counter Fraud Report
findings.headline: No formal process exists for deciding which detected fraud cases to publicize, limiting deterrence
findings.detail: While the Council publicizes some cases of detected fraud leading to criminal conviction or in the public interest, it does not have an agreed process to decide which cases to publicize. The auditor found this absence limits deterrence and public awareness of the Council's success in detecting fraud.
findings.matters: Without publicizing fraud cases consistently, the deterrent effect is weakened and potential fraudsters may underestimate detection risk and consequences
findings.figures: No agreed approach to decide which fraud cases to publicize
findings.quote: The Council does not have an agreed process to decide which cases to publicise. The absence of an agreed approach can limit deterrence and public awareness of the Council's success in detecting fraud.

findings.paper_title: 06 (3 of 3) - Appendix 2 AW Swansea Counter Fraud Report
findings.headline: Counter-fraud efforts are predominantly reactive investigations with no resources allocated for proactive prevention measures
findings.detail: The Council's efforts are primarily focused on reactive investigations with limited focus on proactive prevention of fraud. Its Anti-Fraud Plan does not include provision or identify resources for planned preventative counter fraud works, and there is no clear link between identified fraud risks and mitigating actions.
findings.matters: A reactive-only approach means fraud may go undetected for extended periods, potentially resulting in greater financial losses and demonstrating insufficient preventative controls
findings.figures: Anti-Fraud Plan does not include resources for preventative works; no link between fraud risks and mitigating actions
findings.quote: Overall, however, we found that the Council's efforts are primarily focussed on reactive investigations. It has a limited focus on proactive prevention of fraud. For example, its Anti-Fraud Plan does not include provision or identify resources for planned proactive or preventative counter fraud works. There is no clear link between fraud risks identified in the Fraud Risk Assessment and mitigating actions in the Anti-Fraud Plan.

findings.paper_title: 06 (3 of 3) - Appendix 2 AW Swansea Counter Fraud Report
findings.headline: Counter-fraud training uptake is extremely low with only 24 staff trained and no mandatory requirement
findings.detail: The Council's counter fraud training is not mandatory and uptake is very low. At the time of audit, only 24 members of staff had completed the training module. The auditor noted it is important that staff and councillors are regularly trained to help ensure awareness of how to spot and report fraud.
findings.matters: With so few staff trained and training not mandatory, most employees lack awareness of counter-fraud arrangements and ability to spot and report fraud, creating a significant control weakness
findings.figures: Only 24 staff members have completed counter-fraud training
findings.quote: The Council provides counter fraud training but its current approach is not effective. The training is not mandatory and uptake is very low – at the time of our review, only 24 members of staff had completed the training module.

findings.paper_title: 06 (3 of 3) - Appendix 2 AW Swansea Counter Fraud Report
findings.headline: Council has no formally approved Fraud Response Plan to guide investigation and response procedures
findings.detail: The Council does not have a formally approved Fraud Response Plan or equivalent that clearly sets out its arrangements to identify, respond to, and manage fraud risks. Without this, there is no assurance that fraud investigations are handled consistently or in compliance with defined procedures.
findings.matters: Without a formal response plan, fraud investigations may be handled inconsistently, potentially compromising evidence integrity and the Council's ability to recover losses
findings.figures: No formally approved Fraud Response Plan exists
findings.quote: The Council does not have a formally approved Fraud Response Plan, or equivalent, that clearly sets out its arrangements to identify, respond to, and manage fraud risks.

findings.paper_title: 06 (3 of 3) - Appendix 2 AW Swansea Counter Fraud Report
findings.headline: Fraud risk assessment does not include service area managers, limiting identification of fraud risks across the organisation
findings.detail: Although the Corporate Fraud Team completes the annual Fraud Risk Assessment, service area managers are not engaged in this process. The auditor found this could limit how comprehensively the risk of fraud is assessed throughout the organisation.
findings.matters: Without input from managers across all service areas, the Council may fail to identify fraud risks specific to those areas, leaving control gaps unaddressed
findings.figures: Service area managers excluded from Fraud Risk Assessment process
findings.quote: However, service area managers are not engaged in this process. This could limit how comprehensively the risk of fraud is assessed throughout the organisation.

findings.paper_title: 06 (3 of 3) - Appendix 2 AW Swansea Counter Fraud Report
findings.headline: Anti-fraud and Corruption Policy has not been updated since 2016 and does not reflect current legislation or fraud risks
findings.detail: The Council's policy setting out its zero-tolerance stance and planned response to fraud was last updated a decade ago. The auditor found it is important that the Council reviews and updates its policies to ensure they are relevant, appropriate and reflect current legislation and current fraud risks.
findings.matters: An outdated policy that does not reflect current fraud methods and risks undermines the Council's ability to prevent and detect fraud effectively, creating a control weakness
findings.figures: Policy last updated in 2016
findings.quote: The Policy, which was last updated in 2016, is supported by an annual Anti-Fraud Plan. It is important that the Council reviews and updates its policies to ensure that they are relevant, appropriate and reflect current legislation and the current fraud risks.

findings.headline: Council embedded refined savings tracker in routine reporting to improve delivery visibility and mitigation planning
findings.detail: The council has implemented an enhanced savings delivery monitoring framework with a refined tracker now embedded in routine reporting cycles. This provides improved oversight of whether planned savings are being realised, with stronger mitigation planning when delivery is at risk.
findings.matters: Credible savings tracking and active mitigation are essential indicators that a council will meet its financial targets; this shows awareness of delivery risk.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The Council has strengthened the monitoring of savings delivery through an enhanced reporting framework. The refined savings tracker is now embedded within routine reporting cycles, supporting improved oversight, stronger mitigation planning and more transparent reporting to Members.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs being addressed through in-house provision expansion and B&B reduction
findings.detail: The council has opened Llys Glas facility and a second large-scale temporary supported accommodation scheme is scheduled for early 2027. Active work is underway to reduce reliance on bed-and-breakfast placements, with additional Rapid Rehousing workers recruited to support transitions to permanent housing and improve move-on rates.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is typically the most volatile council budget line; this council is making capital investments to manage costs, but the ongoing pressure is acknowledged as a strategic risk.
findings.figures: Llys Glas operational; second scheme opens early 2027
findings.quote: Llys Glas is now fully operational, and progress has been made on the second large-scale temporary supported accommodation scheme which is due to open early 2027. The existing Rapid Rehousing Plan addendum remains focused on reducing reliance on Bed and Breakfast.

findings.headline: Single-year government funding settlements continue to constrain longer-term financial planning
findings.detail: The council's progress on longer-term financial planning remains limited by the annual cycle of government funding allocations, with additional uncertainty from the Welsh Government's failed supplementary budget and pending UK government decisions. The Medium-Term Financial Plan continues to be refreshed only annually as a result.
findings.matters: Inability to plan beyond one year limits strategic capital and service decisions; compounded by government budget delays, this creates material refinancing risk for a lender reviewing the council's forward position.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Progress in longer-term financial planning remains constrained by the continued use of single-year funding settlements at national level. Welsh Government failed to pass supplementary budget adds to uncertainty, while we also wait for UK governments decision on budgets.

findings.paper_title: 04 (5 of 7) - Appendix 3 - Internal Audit Annual Plan 2026&27 status at 30-06-26
findings.headline: Capital programme audit commissioned by CMT following an external PPA recommendation
findings.detail: A new audit has been added to review the controls and governance in the council's capital programme, explicitly noted as requested by CMT and following a PPA recommendation. This indicates external review bodies have identified concerns about how the capital programme is managed.
findings.matters: External recommendations for capital governance audits typically indicate concerns about scheme delivery, cost control or financial controls, which affects the council's ability to deliver forecast capital investment.
findings.figures: Audit allocated 15 days
findings.quote: New audit requested by CMT to review the controls and governance in place around the Council's capital programme. (PPA Recommendation).

findings.paper_title: 04 (5 of 7) - Appendix 3 - Internal Audit Annual Plan 2026&27 status at 30-06-26
findings.headline: Council has identified directorate overspending issues and commissioned a new audit on cost control
findings.detail: A new audit called 'Maintaining Financial Control' has been added to the plan to review the council's approach to cost control and sign-off processes in directorates. The audit scope explicitly references directorates with 'overspending patterns', indicating this is a known issue affecting multiple service areas.
findings.matters: Directorate overspending signals budget control weaknesses and indicates ongoing financial management challenges, which is a key metric for assessing the council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: Audit allocated 10 days
findings.quote: Review of approach to cost control and sign off in directorate especially those with overspending patterns, even if outside of their control due to demand.

findings.paper_title: 05 Finance Directorate Risk Management Arrangements and Key Risks
findings.headline: Senior finance officer position held on interim basis, indicating gap in permanent leadership
findings.detail: The report is authored by Simon Arthurs, identified as Interim Head of Finance, Deputy Section 151 Officer. The Section 151 Officer—the statutory chief finance officer—is either vacant or the permanent holder is not in post.
findings.matters: The Section 151 Officer is statutorily accountable for the council's financial administration and strategy; an interim arrangement indicates a gap in permanent senior finance leadership
findings.figures: Report authored by Simon Arthurs, Interim Head of Finance, Deputy Section 151 Officer
findings.quote: Report Author & Job Title: Simon Arthurs, Interim Head of Finance, Deputy Section 151 Officer

findings.paper_title: 05 Finance Directorate Risk Management Arrangements and Key Risks
findings.headline: Accounts receivable debt collection audit weakness; project to address it remains open
findings.detail: A project to improve debt collection was initiated following an unsatisfactory audit report outcome. The audit rating has improved to 'substantial', but the project continues. The directorate is establishing additional performance KPIs during 2026/27 and expects to close the project risk once these have been tracked through the year.
findings.matters: Debt collection is critical to council cash flow and financial health; an unsatisfactory audit finding indicates past control weaknesses in income collection, and the remediation remains incomplete
findings.figures: Audit rating improved to: substantial
findings.quote: The project formed part of the mitigation to an unsatisfactory audit report outcome. A significant amount of work has been completed and the most recent audit report rating is substantial. A more detailed suite of performance KPI's are being established as part of the 2026/27 Finance Service plan and once in place and tracked to the end of the financial year it is anticipated the project risk will then be closed.

findings.paper_title: 04 (2 of 7) - Appendix A - Q1 2026&27 Monitoring Report Redacted
findings.headline: Two audits received Moderate assurance ratings, indicating control weaknesses were found
findings.detail: Two of the 15 audits finalised in Q1 were rated Moderate assurance (13% of total), meaning control gaps were identified. The specific issues identified are detailed in an exempt section of the committee papers and not disclosed here.
findings.matters: Moderate assurance means controls are not operating reliably in those areas. A lender needs to know what control weaknesses exist and whether management has plans to fix them.
findings.figures: 2 moderate assurance audits out of 15 finalised (13%)
findings.quote: Two audit report were issued with a Moderate Assurance rating in the quarter. The key issues for each audit is summarised in the exempt section of the agenda pack.

findings.paper_title: 04 (2 of 7) - Appendix A - Q1 2026&27 Monitoring Report Redacted
findings.headline: Senior auditor retirement and vacancy cost the audit function approximately 57 days of capacity in Q1
findings.detail: A senior auditor retired in late April 2026. Although the role was filled internally through promotion, the vacancy and transition resulted in approximately 57 days of audit capacity being lost in the first quarter. A second vacancy (for an auditor post) has since been filled.
findings.matters: Internal audit is the council's primary mechanism for identifying control failures and financial irregularities. Significant staffing gaps directly reduce audit coverage and the council's ability to detect problems.
findings.figures: approximately 57 days lost in the quarter due to vacancies
findings.quote: However, one senior auditor retired in late April. The senior auditor post was ringfenced internally within the team, and an experienced auditor was successfully appointed. However, approximately 57 days have been lost in the quarter due to vacancies.

findings.headline: Housing Benefits & Council Tax Reduction system rated Substantial with 15 outstanding recommendations
findings.detail: Despite receiving a Substantial assurance rating, testing of Housing Benefits & Council Tax Reduction (a fundamental system) identified 9 lower-risk recommendations and 6 governance/process recommendations across multiple tested areas. No major-risk findings, but the volume of process recommendations suggests multiple control or procedural gaps.
findings.matters: A major financial system administering benefits to residents carries operational risk; multiple process recommendations indicate areas where controls are not yet optimized
findings.figures: 9 lower-risk recommendations; 6 governance/process recommendations
findings.quote: No MR rec's noted but 9 LR recs and 6 GP recommendations noted across a number of areas tested warranting a Substial Assurance rating.

findings.paper_title: 04 (4 of 7) - Appendix 2 - Audit Scope Q1 2026&27 Redacted
findings.headline: Primary Schools Unofficial Fund control weakness repeated from previous audit—single signatory on cheques
findings.detail: Testing of school unofficial funds found one school had only one signatory required on cheques when best practice and procedures require two. This finding is explicitly marked as repeated, meaning it was raised in a prior audit and the school has not corrected it.
findings.matters: Unresolved control weakness in fund handling across audit cycles indicates schools or council may not be implementing governance recommendations; opens fraud or misuse risk
findings.figures: 1 school in sample; 6 of 7 recommendations in this audit were repeated
findings.quote: There should be an appropriate number of signatories for the account and cheques issued should be signed by two authorised signatories. Our testing found that for one school, only one signatory was required on cheques (MR).

findings.paper_title: 04 (4 of 7) - Appendix 2 - Audit Scope Q1 2026&27 Redacted
findings.headline: Streetworks mileage verification issue persists from previous audit cycle without resolution
findings.detail: Testing found multiple instances where location details were not recorded accurately, preventing verification of claimed mileage. The audit report explicitly marks this as a Repeated MR recommendation, indicating the same issue was raised before and not fixed.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit findings signal that management may not be implementing recommendations; a pattern across multiple departments of expense control weakness
findings.figures: Multiple instances in sample testing; marked as Repeated
findings.quote: Sample testing of mileage claims revealed several insances where location details had not been recorded accurately to allow the mielage claimed to be verified (Repeated MR rec).

findings.paper_title: 04 (4 of 7) - Appendix 2 - Audit Scope Q1 2026&27 Redacted
findings.headline: Mileage claims in Youth Justice Service appear to be overstated
findings.detail: Testing of employee mileage claims identified two instances where claims could not be verified as correct and appeared to be overstated. Officers attributed this to either incomplete journey recording or claiming multiple journeys as a single amount.
findings.matters: Systematic expense verification weakness could indicate either poor controls or deliberate fraud; suggests management may not have tight oversight of staff expenditure
findings.figures: 2 employees with overstated mileage claims; claims in Youth Justice audit
findings.quote: Sample testing of mileage claims revealed claims for two employees could not be verified as correct with claims appearing to be overstated.

findings.paper_title: 10 (5 of 5) Appendix D Swansea CEO Letter to Audit Wales -SOA
findings.headline: Recovery plan in place to return to statutory timelines by 2026/27, with 2025/26 draft statements already submitted
findings.detail: Swansea is working with Audit Wales on a formal recovery plan, with agreed improvements for 2025/26 and a target return to normal statutory timelines for 2026/27. Draft signed statements for 2025/26 have already been submitted ahead of the recovery plan schedule.
findings.matters: Compliance with audit regulator oversight and execution of recovery plans indicate how management is addressing control failures and capacity issues
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: Consequently, we have worked with Audit Wales colleagues throughout this period and continue to do so in relation to 2025/26, where we have agreed an improved position as we work back to the statutory timelines for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 10 (5 of 5) Appendix D Swansea CEO Letter to Audit Wales -SOA
findings.headline: Swansea missed statutory deadlines for 2024/25 accounts filing
findings.detail: The council did not meet statutory timelines for completing, auditing and filing the Statement of Accounts for 2024/25. The council states it maintained high quality standards despite the delay, and has increased finance leadership capacity to prevent future misses.
findings.matters: Timely statutory accounts filing is a material control and transparency issue; lenders depend on current, audited financial reporting to assess credit risk
findings.quote: We also acknowledge that we have not met the statutory timelines in 2024/25, although we have maintained the high quality, despite a significant increase in technical changes.

findings.headline: £21.466m unsupported borrowing in 2025/26 capital programme; interest rate risk flagged as high priority
findings.detail: Of £146.113m capital spend financed in 2025/26, £21.466m was raised through unsupported borrowing (General Fund and HRA combined), with £6.336m through supported borrowing.
