The capital risk register identifies 'Interest Rates' as an 'A' level (high) risk with mitigation described as 'Timing of locking in borrowing. Market analysis.' This indicates the council does not yet have certainty over borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Unsupported borrowing expands the council's long-term debt burden and interest rate exposure. For a lender, the council's flagged concern about timing and market conditions suggests incomplete hedging or price certainty for the capital programme, creating a budget risk that could affect financial resilience.
findings.figures: £21.466m unsupported borrowing; £6.336m supported borrowing; £27.802m total borrowing (19% of £146.113m to be funded)
findings.quote: Unsupported Borrowing (GF plus HRA)    21,466

findings.headline: £7m of Debenhams acquisition project budget reclassified and moved to contingency mid-year; project value restated from £13.351m
findings.detail: The City Centre Acquisitions (Debenhams) project had an estimated value of £13.351m. Due to negotiation changes where 'the letting landlord will now fit out' rather than the council, £7m was reclassified as savings and transferred to finance contingency for review 'once the Q1 position is known.' The remaining £6.351m sits underspent. The council explicitly states this £7m adjustment was required to meet its 80% delivery target.
findings.matters: Mid-year budget reclassifications to meet delivery targets suggest either the initial estimate was incorrect or delivery scope is not yet defined. For a lender, this indicates forecasting reliability issues or unresolved project terms, both of which increase cost overrun risk.
findings.figures: £13.351m estimated value; £7m moved to contingency for future review; £6.351m underspent; reclassification needed to meet 80% target
findings.quote: £7m savings on the Debenhams scheme have been moved back to programme contingency within Finance for future consideration once the Q1 position is known. With the inclusion of £7million variation from Debenhams, the target of 80% is met.

findings.headline: Three major projects experiencing significant delays: Skyline (£4.265m underspent), Bascule Bridge (£2.778m), Lower Swansea Valley (£3.394m)
findings.detail: Multiple major schemes show substantial slippage with specific delivery obstacles. Skyline was delayed by unmet conditions precedent in the Agreement for Lease, preventing land acquisitions and council highway works. Bascule Bridge faced contractual delays. Lower Swansea Valley was held up while enabling works packages were commissioned to build cost certainty before main contract entry.
findings.matters: Major project delays on infrastructure and regeneration schemes indicate delivery or contractual risks. For a lender, delays on schemes involving land acquisition and highway infrastructure signal potential supplier, market, or legal risks that could extend repayment timelines and affect asset values.
findings.figures: Skyline £4.265m underspent; Bascule Bridge £2.778m underspent; Lower Swansea Valley £3.394m underspent
findings.quote: Skyline's delay in satisfying the conditions precedent within the Agreement for Lease prevented the Council from progressing key elements of the project. Until conditionality was reached, the Council was unable to complete associated land acquisitions, including air rights, or commence delivery of Council-led highway works.

findings.headline: Capital programme achieved £152.994m outturn against revised budget of £200.739m, leaving £47.745m underspent and carried forward
findings.detail: The council's capital programme resulted in net underspending of £47.745m (23.8% of revised budget). Major slippage occurred across directorates: Place £36.313m, HRA £8.718m, Education £3.462m, and Finance contingency £7.567m. The paper describes this as 'a combination of underspending/overspending and slippage' from projects in progress that will continue or draw on capital contingency to meet unavoidable cost pressures.
findings.matters: For a lender, capital delivery is a core performance metric. Underspends at this scale (nearly one quarter of the revised budget) signal potential execution difficulties, forecasting challenges, or programme management issues that could affect the council's ability to deliver strategic priorities and manage debt-funded schemes.
findings.figures: £47.745m underspend; £200.739m revised budget; £152.994m outturn; Place £36.313m; HRA £8.718m; Education £3.462m
findings.quote: Capital outturn in 2025/2026 total £152.994m based on the revised approved budget of £200.739m.

findings.headline: Dependency on one-off grant funding creates sustainability risk for 2026/27
findings.detail: Additional Learning Needs pressures are being offset by grant awards that 'have been continuous for a few years', but the S151 notes 'there is still concern that the funding could end with little notice'. The report warns these grants are not expected to recur and 'forecast pressures will return' in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Using non-recurrent grant income to balance recurrent budgets is a red flag. When grants cease, councils face cliff-edge budget pressures. The S151 is already flagging this risk.
findings.figures: ALN grant funding provides relief to budget but is non-guaranteed; several directorates identifying 'significant underspends are either grants that could disappear'
findings.quote: While these grants have been continuous for a few years, there is still concern that the funding could end with little notice. Moving into 2026/27, it is expected that many of the above reported underspends are either grants that could disappear or savings which have been fully utilised so our forecast pressures will return.

findings.headline: Treasury management strategy creates future borrowing cost risk as fixed-rate debt matures
findings.detail: The council locked in historically low fixed-rate PWLB debt in early years of the capital programme, before base rate rises. Cash is now invested at elevated variable rates. A £4.9m capital financing underspend in 2025/26 resulted. However, as cash balances are drawn down and early fixed-rate debt matures, refinancing will occur at much higher rates while variable rate investment income falls, creating a material cost squeeze.
findings.matters: The council is benefiting from favorable debt/cash arbitrage now, but this is temporary. Future net financing costs will rise materially as the debt maturity ladder rolls and cash depletes. This is baked into the medium-term forecast but represents growing debt servicing pressure.
findings.figures: Capital financing underspend 2025/26: £4.88m; net interest charges fell from £18.3m budget to £12.7m actual (-30.8%); benefit is temporary
findings.quote: Net financing costs will likely rise significantly in future as set out in the medium-term financial plan, as cash balances are drawn down and variable interest rates begin to drop whereas debt is fixed (albeit at low rates).

findings.headline: Council tax reduction scheme demand growing; council holds unlimited financial risk
findings.detail: CTRS is an uncapped, demand-led service where the council bears all demand risk and all tax-base risk. If council tax rises, CTRS cost rises and the council funds the full increase. Economic uncertainty and cost-of-living pressures are expected to drive demand up. The scheme underspent by only £121k in 2025/26 despite budget assumptions of 20% take-up shortfall.
findings.matters: CTRS is a structural exposure to economic downturns. If unemployment or cost-of-living crises intensify, this demand-led scheme has unlimited downside that immediately impacts the council's net income.
findings.figures: CTRS underspend 2025/26: £121k; scheme 80% funded by WG block grant (fixed), 20% by council (demand-exposed); budget based on assumed non-take-up
findings.quote: Growing economic uncertainty (cost of living concerns, recent re-emerging inflation pressures, geopolitical uncertainty spilling over into potentially wider slowing economic activity) means there is the likelihood of demand and CTRS spend and now increasing also discretionary housing allowance spend rising significantly over time and this may continue to exceed budget in future years.

findings.headline: Inflation embedded in base budgets; headline rates have fallen but costs remain elevated
findings.detail: The council notes that 40-year-high inflation rates 'which were never funded even as headline annual rates have now come down significantly, remain cumulative embedded pressures in ongoing base budgets'. This is a structural issue: nominal budget increases are not sufficient to cover the embedded cost base.
findings.matters: Even if headline inflation falls, the embedded elevated cost base persists. Real-terms budget cuts are disguised as nominal increases, forcing difficult choices about service levels or debt.
findings.figures: Headline inflation fell significantly from 2022-23 peaks; but cumulative embedded pressures remain in base budgets unaddressed
findings.quote: Those recent previous 40-year high inflation levels (including service, general and energy inflation) which were never funded even as headline annual rates have now come down significantly, remain cumulative embedded pressures in ongoing base budgets.

findings.headline: Council drew £43m from reserves in 2025/26; S151 states trajectory is "clearly not sustainable" medium to long term
findings.detail: The council drew roughly £43m from reserves in 2025/26. This was driven by £13m for the equal pay provision, heavy use of the capital equalisation reserve to avoid locking in new borrowing at 'prohibitive' rates, and school deficits. The S151 acknowledges this is 'clearly not on a sustainable trajectory in the medium to longer term'.
findings.matters: A £43m draw from reserves in a single year is unsustainable. Councils do not generate reserves annually; this rate of draw exhausts them in 2-3 years absent budget recovery.
findings.figures: Net draw from reserves 2025/26: ~£43m including £13m equal pay, £23.1m capital equalisation, £6.1m schools; carries forward £2.9m to reserves
findings.quote: The Council is also spending significant elements of its admittedly deliberately large working capital, fully short term financed by further draws from cash backed reserves... The draws from reserves and cash to temporarily fund capital will continue to grow significantly during 2026/27 and are clearly not on a sustainable trajectory in the medium to longer term.

findings.headline: Planned savings only 73% achieved; £4.8m gap closed with one-off mitigations
findings.detail: Target was £13.97m in savings; only £10.22m delivered by year-end (73%). The council states 'Where savings have not been fully achieved within 2025/26 a range of mitigating measures have been put in place including relying on one off other actions' to show 100% achievement. This masks structural underperformance against agreed savings plans.
findings.matters: Persistent miss against savings targets indicates either unrealistic planning or inability to deliver. Relying on one-offs to plug gaps is unsustainable and signals the budget assumptions are breaking down.
findings.figures: Savings target 2025/26: £13.97m; delivered: £10.22m (73%); gap: £3.75m closed by temporary mitigations; overall achieved: 100% (on paper)
findings.quote: Against a savings target of £13.974m, £10.223m or some 73% has been achieved by 31st March. It should be noted that where savings have not been fully achieved within 2025/26 a range of mitigating measures have been put in place including relying on one off other actions.

findings.headline: Adult social care sustained overspend across all major commissioned service lines
findings.detail: Adult Services overspent by £6.1m. Residential care for older persons overspent £1.9m, domiciliary care £1.3m, learning disability £2.4m, younger adults £1.1m. These are demand-led services where prices are rising faster than budgets can track. The directorate faced 'sustained financial pressure' driven by 'demand-led, legal and inflationary pressures across commissioned care services'.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest service budget and persistently overshoots. Lenders worry about councils losing control of demand-led budgets. This is now structural—demand and inflation are outpacing budget provision.
findings.figures: Adult Services overspend: £6.08m; residential older persons: £1.9m; domiciliary care: £1.3m; learning disability: £2.4m; younger adults: £1.1m
findings.quote: The directorate faced sustained financial pressure throughout the year, driven primarily by demand-led, legal and inflationary pressures across commissioned care services.

findings.headline: Schools reserves fell from £18.3m to £12.1m in 2025/26; secondary reserves down 60.96% over three years
findings.detail: Schools carried over a combined £18.3m in reserves at 31/3/2025; by 31/3/2026 this fell to £12.1m (£6.1m spend in a single year). Secondary school reserves especially fragile, down from £6.5m to £3.2m (60.96% fall). Schools overspent their delegated budget by £6.1m (2.87%). The S151 warns that schools are expected to draw reserves again significantly in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Schools reserves are the council's second line of defense but are depleting rapidly due to sustained overspends against rising budgets. This will worsen pressure on core statutory services when reserves are exhausted.
findings.figures: Schools total reserves: £18.3m (31/3/2025) to £12.1m (31/3/2026); secondary: £6.5m to £3.2m (-60.96%); primary: £11.4m to £8.8m (-21.88%); schools overspend 2025/26: £6.14m
findings.quote: During 2025/26 Schools expenditure overall was £6,140,359 more than the delegated budget, equating to an overspend of approximately 2.87%... It is expected, given the above reserve position that the outturn position for 2026/27 for schools, will evidence a further net call on existing reserves, even after allowing for £12.262m of additional funding provided.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve drawn by £4m in 2025/26; S151 states no scope for additional expenditure
findings.detail: The council drew £4m from General Reserves in 2025/26 to fund the equal pay increase. The S151 Officer explicitly states the General Fund Reserve is now considered very low for the council's size, and has written that there is no scope within the reduced General reserves to fund any additional expenditure given identified risks.
findings.matters: A council with no general reserve buffer cannot absorb demand shocks in adult social care, homelessness, or waste management—all identified as ongoing overspend risks for 2026/27. This forces use of earmarked reserves or service cuts.
findings.figures: £4m drawn from General Reserves in 2025/26; General Fund Reserve now at minimum acceptable level; S151 states no scope for further expenditure
findings.quote: It should be noted that the General Fund Reserve, is now considered very low for the size of this Council... It is the opinion of the Section 151 Officer at this point that there is no scope within the reduced General reserves to fund any additional expenditure of the Council.

findings.headline: Equal pay provision increased by £13m to £28m with further unquantified contingent liabilities
findings.detail: The S151 Officer increased the general equal pay provision from £15m to £28m immediately, reflecting crystallization of long-standing single status pay appeals. The report explicitly discloses additional unpriced contingent liabilities of uncertain value and timing that could require further provision. The figure itself may change until accounts are signed off and audited.
findings.matters: Equal pay represents a material crystallizing liability with further downside risk. The £13m provision increase was funded by drawing down General Reserves, directly constraining future debt capacity and forcing future budgets to repay this draw while managing equal pay risk.
findings.figures: Equal pay provision: £15m to £28m (£13m increase); unpriced contingent liabilities disclosed; figure may change pre-audit; further risk if provision increases or settlement agreed
findings.quote: The general equal pay provision has been assessed by the S151 Officer as needing to be increased from £15m to £28m immediately as a minimum and additional liabilities may exist which are uncertain as to value and will thus be disclosed as "unpriced" contingent liabilities in the statement of accounts.

findings.headline: Service delivery review is underway but 2026/27 budgets have already been increased to reflect ongoing cost pressures
findings.detail: A working group with specialist advisors is conducting a comprehensive review of housing service delivery to improve efficiency. However, rather than wait for the review findings, the council has already increased 2026/27 budgets to reflect ongoing pressures, suggesting management does not expect material savings.
findings.matters: A pending efficiency review paired with forward budget increases (rather than hold) signals the council has low confidence in finding savings; this indicates structural cost inflation, not temporary spikes.
findings.figures: No specific savings target or efficiency gain stated
findings.quote: A working group is currently undertaking a comprehensive review of service delivery, following the engagement of specialist advisors to support the process, with the aim of improving efficiency and informing future planning. Budgets for 2026/27 have also been increased to reflect the ongoing demands and pressures facing the service.

findings.headline: Increased capital contribution of £3.8m funded from reserves to avoid borrowing, accelerating reserve depletion
findings.detail: The council increased its contribution to capital expenditure by £3.81m (beyond plan), enabled by lower housing management costs and reserve use. This avoided any need for external borrowing, but it means capital investment was funded by drawing down reserves rather than from revenue or borrowing.
findings.matters: Funding capital from reserves rather than revenue or borrowing is unsustainable; it shifts the funding burden to future years and compounds reserve depletion pressure.
findings.figures: Increased contribution to capital expenditure £3.810m; total revenue funding for capital schemes £27.734m actual vs £23.924m revised budget
findings.quote: The increased contribution to capital expenditure is attributable to a number of factors. Despite slippage in the 2025/26 Capital Programme, lower housing management costs and the use of reserves enabled a higher contribution, resulting in no requirement for external borrowing.

findings.headline: HRA reserves drawn £1.454m in 2025/26, with further £4.488m budgeted for 2026/27 transfer
findings.detail: Reserves opened the year at £16.633m and closed at £15.179m after the 2025/26 deficit transfer. A further £4.488m is already budgeted to be transferred from reserves in 2026/27, bringing the forecast closing balance to £10.691m. This is a £6m reduction over two consecutive years.
findings.matters: Accelerating reserve drawdowns reduce financial flexibility and resilience; large committed future transfers signal the council is managing cash rather than finances, and any income shortfall or unexpected cost creates immediate borrowing need.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £16.633m; closing 2025/26 £15.179m; budgeted 2026/27 transfer £4.488m; forecast closing 2026/27 £10.691m
findings.quote: The opening balance for the year was £16.633m. With the final 2025/26 transfer from reserves of £1.454m, the closing balance is £15.179m.

findings.headline: Revenue repairs overran by £5.3m, with responsive repairs up £3.4m due to sustained demand despite mid-year budget increase
findings.detail: The repairs budget was increased at year start but still overran by £5.3m. Responsive repairs alone exceeded budget by £3.4m, driven by OFS appointment scheduling, damp and mould work, tenant engagement, complaints handling, increased inspections, and improved record-keeping. Voids cost £1.1m extra and electrical and gas maintenance together added £593k.
findings.matters: Large overspends in routine maintenance point to either deferred problems catching up, or structural cost inflation; the council expected these after increasing budgets mid-year, suggesting the problems are not temporary.
findings.figures: Revenue repairs overspend £5.322m; responsive repairs £3.4m; voids £1.1m; electrical £283k; gas £310k
findings.quote: The revenue repairs budget was increased at the start of the year; however, significant additional pressures persisted, particularly in day-to-day responsive repairs due to sustained demand and service developments.

findings.headline: HRA swung from budgeted £5.352m surplus to £1.454m deficit, a £6.8m adverse movement
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account showed a significant variance to plan. The originally budgeted surplus of £5.352m became an actual deficit of £1.454m, requiring the transfer to be reversed and funded from reserves instead. This represents a £6.806m adverse movement year-on-year.
findings.matters: A £6.8m forecast error or control failure indicates either weak budgeting discipline or unexpected cost pressures; either way, it signals financial fragility and risk to future plans.
findings.figures: Original budgeted surplus £5.352m; actual deficit £1.454m; total adverse movement £6.806m
findings.quote: The HRA showed a deficit of £1.454m compared with the original budgeted surplus as outlined in the budget report to members on 6th March 2025 of £5.352m.

findings.paper_title: 11 (2 of 2) - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Internal audit team lost approximately 220 days to sickness absence in 2025/26, impacting audit plan completion to 82%
findings.detail: The Internal Audit Team operated in a challenging environment in 2025/26 with approximately 220 days lost to sickness absence. Only 82% of the 122-activity audit plan was completed by year end, though 89% was completed or in progress. The Chief Auditor noted the team worked tirelessly despite resource constraints to complete as much as possible.
findings.matters: Incomplete internal audit coverage creates gaps in the council's assurance over controls and financial systems. High sickness absence suggests operational stress and potential sustainability issues in the control environment.
findings.figures: 220 days sickness absence; 82 of 122 audit activities completed (82% completion); 89% completed or in progress
findings.quote: The Internal Audit Team has continued to operate in a very challenging environment throughout 2025/26. Approximately 220 days were lost to sickness absence.

findings.paper_title: 11 (2 of 2) - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Medium-term financial planning relies on uncertain government finance settlements in challenging public spending outlook
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan for 2027-30 was approved by Council in March 2026 but was prepared in a challenging outlook for public spending and uncertainty over the national budget. The council's strategy depends on the scale and value of future local government finance settlements. Although the council currently sees no indication that assets may need to be impaired, the forward planning explicitly acknowledges reliance on government funding decisions that remain unannounced.
findings.matters: A council's ability to meet its obligations and service debt depends on stable or growing income. If government finance settlements contract materially or are delayed, the council may face difficult choices between service delivery and debt service.
findings.figures: MTFP covers 2027-30 period; no impairment expected at present
findings.quote: All spending and funding assumptions were set in a challenging outlook for public spending and public services and against the backdrop of uncertainty setting the national budget. Whilst the Authority will consider future spending plans in line with projected funding announcements and revised cash limits there is no indication at present that any of the assets of the Authority may be impaired as a result of a need to close facilities and reduce the level of service provision.

findings.paper_title: 11 (2 of 2) - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council faces uncertainty over scale of additional spending and funding arrangements needed in response to economic outlook
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer has advised that the council faces possible risks and uncertainties regarding additional spending, loss of income, and funding arrangements for reimbursement. The statement explicitly acknowledges it remains unclear what the scale of additional spending will be and how much will be reimbursed. This reflects exposure to geopolitical tensions, trade uncertainties, and wider economic aftershocks.
findings.matters: Unquantified exposure to additional spending and income loss creates material uncertainty in the financial forecast. The council's ability to respond to this undefined position directly affects financial resilience and borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Not quantified in document
findings.quote: It remains unclear as to the scale of additional spending, the loss of income, and the funding arrangements for reimbursement in part, or in full, that the Authority faces in responding both locally, with partners, and supporting the national strategic response to the economic outlook.

findings.paper_title: 11 (2 of 2) - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: New risk management system introduced March 2025 showing early inconsistencies, with improvements to be monitored through 2026-27
findings.detail: The council revised risk management arrangements in 2024 and introduced a new risk management system in late March 2025. A review by Audit Wales identified inconsistencies in early application of these revised arrangements and made recommendations for improvement aligned with previous internal audit findings. The council committed to monitoring implementation of these recommendations throughout 2026-27.
findings.matters: Inconsistent application of risk management undermines the council's ability to identify, assess and control material financial and operational risks. This is foundational to effective governance and financial management.
findings.figures: Risk management system introduced March 2025; review conducted December 2025
findings.quote: Following a review of risk management arrangements undertaken by Audit Wales, a number of inconsistencies in the early application of the revised arrangements were identified. Several recommendations for improvement were made which were in line with previous internal audit findings. The implementation of the recommendations will be monitored throughout 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 11 (2 of 2) - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Capital programme governance has identified weaknesses requiring remedial action in 2026-27
findings.detail: The council has identified ongoing weaknesses in capital programme and contract management, including inconsistent project governance maturity and variability in delivery. The governance statement explicitly lists this as a Significant Governance Issue requiring action in 2026-27. Actions planned include embedding a revised capital governance model, implementing a consistent contract management framework, and strengthening corporate-level monitoring of capital programmes.
findings.matters: Capital delivery risk is material to debt service capacity and the council's ability to execute its £50m+ borrowing programme. Weak governance over capital projects and contracts directly impacts cost control and delivery confidence.
findings.figures: Future capital spending plans of up to £50 million; £50m+ financed by unsupported borrowing
findings.quote: The Council has identified ongoing weaknesses in the governance of its capital programme and contract management arrangements. These include inconsistent maturity of project and programme governance, variability in delivery and the need to strengthen contract management practices, including the management of legal, commercial and compliance risks.

findings.headline: A £1 million overstatement of surplus land and buildings assets remains uncorrected in the 2024-25 accounts.
findings.detail: The council recorded £1 million in surplus land and buildings additions for which the lease premium payment was not received in 2024-25, overstating assets by that amount. Though deemed immaterial by audit standards, the council has not corrected it and must provide written justification.
findings.matters: Uncorrected asset misstatements indicate control weaknesses in capital accounting, suggesting the finance function may struggle with complex or non-routine transactions.
findings.figures: £1 million overstatement in surplus land and buildings assets
findings.quote: The Council's land and buildings assets increase by asset additions in the year. However, surplus asset additions included £1 million relating to land for which the lease premium was not received by the Council in 2024-25. This has resulted in the value of surplus land and building assets being overstated by £1 million with a corresponding overstatement to the capital adjustment account.

findings.headline: Swansea has missed accounts delivery deadlines for four consecutive years, with the 2024-25 draft received five months late.
findings.detail: The council agreed to deliver draft accounts by 30 June 2025 but received them on 16 December 2025 after multiple revisions to the deadline. This is the fourth successive year of late delivery, though the 2023-24 accounts came much earlier (9 August 2024). The auditor notes this 'presents a significant challenge for the Council, for us and for stakeholders' and warns that future deadlines are tightening to 30 September for 2025-26 and beyond.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to meet financial reporting deadlines signals underlying resource, capability, or process weakness in the council's finance function, affecting stakeholder confidence and relationships with lenders and funders who depend on timely reporting.
findings.figures: Draft accounts received 16 December 2025 (deadline 30 June 2025); 2023-24 accounts submitted 9 August 2024
findings.quote: Following feedback at the close of the 2023-24 audit, we agreed a delivery plan with the Council to produce the draft 2024-25 accounts by 30 June 2025. This deadline was revised several times, and we received the draft accounts on 16 December 2025. This is the fourth year in succession that the draft accounts have been received later than the deadline and is significantly later than the 2023-24 accounts which were submitted on 9 August 2024.

findings.headline: Regeneration programme needs tenants to mitigate future borrowing costs
findings.detail: The Regeneration Programme control measures include the need to 'secure suitable tenants to occupy at least 50% of Block B alongside the Council to mitigate future borrowing costs'. This signals that borrowing to fund the regeneration scheme carries ongoing cost, and occupancy rates will determine whether that borrowing is justifiable.
findings.matters: A regeneration scheme that requires high tenancy rates to justify its borrowing cost is leveraged to commercial outcomes; failure to let space means debt service falls on the council balance sheet.
findings.figures: Block B occupancy target: minimum 50% by 13 Nov 2027
findings.quote: By practical completion, secure suitable tenants to occupy at least 50% of Block B alongside the Council to mitigate future borrowing costs

findings.headline: Building maintenance backlog is underfunded
findings.detail: A new strategic risk (Q3, to be fully implemented Q4) identifies insufficient budget to bring council buildings to adequate condition and quality. The risk is inherent 12 but target and residual scores are not yet assigned. Control measures include a desktop assessment of 8 key assets by mid-2026.
findings.matters: Growing building maintenance backlogs either signal capital budget is too tight, or that the council is deferring necessary capital spend — both of which constrain operational flexibility and increase future costs.
findings.figures: Inherent score 12; target and residual not yet set
findings.quote: There is a risk that there is insufficient budget to fund all necessary works to bring buildings up to a high standard of condition and quality

findings.headline: Safeguarding services are underfunded relative to statutory minimum
findings.detail: Across children's and adult social services, the council identifies that budget allocation is not aligned with the standard spending assessment needed to maintain minimum safe statutory service levels. The risk is flagged as inherent 25, target 16, residual 16 — among the highest on the register. Controls depend on 'within the Councils overall available financial resources', suggesting funds are constrained.
findings.matters: A council knowingly underfunding safeguarding carries reputational and legal risk; failure to recruit/retain social workers or provide safe care volume can trigger inspection findings, litigation, and political crisis.
findings.figures: Inherent score 25, target 16, residual score 16
findings.quote: Prioritise a sufficient budget allocation more closely aligned with the standard spending assessment (within the Councils overall available financial resources) to maintain the Council meeting at least the minimum level of safe statutory service across children and adult services.

findings.headline: General Fund is unsustainably subsidising temporary accommodation
findings.detail: The council receives insufficient Welsh Government funding for temporary accommodation (B&B and similar), forcing the General Fund to meet the gap. This arrangement is explicitly described as 'not sustainable', and the issue score has remained at 16 throughout 2025. Growing homelessness presentations and inadequate housing supply add to pressure.
findings.matters: Unsustainable use of General Fund reserves to cover statutory housing duties signals either rising need that funding doesn't match, or that reserves are being depleted faster than they should be.
findings.figures: Issue score 16 (consistent Jan-Dec 2025)
findings.quote: The Authority is reliant on funding from Welsh Government to meet its statutory obligations. Currently the level of funding is insufficient given the high numbers, and the General Fund is having to meet the shortfall which is not sustainable.

findings.headline: Waste strategy delays are jeopardising budget savings targets
findings.detail: The new waste strategy implementation is delayed until after the 2027 local elections, putting planned 25/26 and MTFP budget savings at risk unless they are formally removed via a FRAP report. The risk score has risen from 9 to 12 and back to 6, but the underlying delay persists.
findings.matters: If savings identified in the MTFP cannot be achieved as planned, the council will face mid-year shortfalls requiring either further cuts or reserve draws.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (Oct-Dec 2025), previously 9 (Sept 2025)
findings.quote: With the intention that a new strategy will be delayed until post local elections in 2027. This will delay ability to deliver 25/26 budget saving proposals and MTFP saving proposals unless these are removed via the FRAP report.

findings.headline: Council's MTFP faces constrained funding, demographic pressures, pay and price inflation, and "potentially reopened equal pay risks"; residual risk score 20/25
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial plan faces continuing constrained funding, demographic pressures, and pay/price inflation. The document explicitly flags 'potentially reopened equal pay risks across local government' as a threat. Risk remains at 20/25, down only slightly from the inherent score of 25.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver MTFP means the council cannot respond to spending pressures and may face contingent liabilities from equal pay claims that could exhaust reserves.
findings.figures: Inherent score 25, target 15, residual score 20 (stable since June 2025)
findings.quote: If we fail to deliver the Council's MTFP and annual budget then we will not be able to respond appropriately to continuing constrained public finance funding, demographic pressures, increasing demand and pay and price pressures, potentially reopened equal pay risks across local government

findings.headline: HRA cannot find sufficient funding and risk is rising
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account cannot identify additional financial resources from Welsh Government, threatening the More Homes Strategy targets and Welsh Housing Quality Standard obligations. The risk score rose from 9 to 12 between August and December 2025. Council acknowledges it will struggle to deliver on housing commitments under current funding.
findings.matters: A council unable to meet statutory housing standards or deliver its housing strategy signals budget stress and potential borrowing pressure to backfill housing shortfalls.
findings.figures: Inherent risk score 16, target 4, residual score 9 rising to 12 (Aug-Dec 2025)
findings.quote: The Authority is unable to identify significant additional HRA financial resources, including WG funding and therefore will not be able to fully achieve key strategic and political objectives such as targets set under the More Homes Strategy and meet its statutory obligations to maintain the Welsh Housing Quality Standard.

findings.headline: Sustainable base savings remain unfound; structural rebalancing needed but not yet delivered
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that 'it remains imperative that sustainable base budget savings are found to replace in year one-off actions to stabilise the 2025/26 budget ahead of the 2026/27 budget round'. This is framed as an outstanding imperative, not an accomplished task. Social Services transformation plan still in early phase (third quarter of three-year program).
findings.matters: A council that has not found sustainable savings by Q3 is unlikely to find them before the next budget round. This signals that 2026/27 will begin with unresolved pressures and a requirement for either further use of reserves or service cuts.
findings.figures: Social Services overspend driven partly by 'delays in implementing the staffing model needed for our Target Operating Model'
findings.quote: It remains imperative that sustainable base budget savings are found to replace in year one-off actions to stabilise the 2025/26 budget ahead of the 2026/27 budget round.

findings.headline: Rent Allowances overspending as discretionary housing payments exceed DWP funding; persistent pressure expected
findings.detail: Housing Benefit top-ups (discretionary housing payments granted to reduce poverty and hardship) are overspending because rent levels 'in some instances materially exceed allowed levels of reimbursement from DWP'. The council flags this as likely to 'grow and persist' despite not being part of formal budget recovery plans.
findings.matters: This signals real housing stress in the local population. Councils only grant discretionary housing payments when statutory support is insufficient. Persistent shortfalls indicate either deteriorating affordability or a growing population in need.
findings.figures: Rent Allowances overspend £0.470m
findings.quote: Rent payable, whilst justifiable, is beginning in some instances to materially exceed allowed levels of reimbursement from DWP which adds to the local burden. Previously we have managed as part of general over and under spending but this pressure is likely to grow and persist.

findings.headline: Planning fee income underperforming; national fee increase may not close the gap
findings.detail: Planning fee income 'continues to underperform against budgeted expectations'. The council notes that 'the national fee increase is now implemented and should improve the position for future years' but this is conditional language. Economic Regeneration overspending £1.051m at Q3.
findings.matters: Development activity is a leading indicator of local economic health. Persistent planning income shortfalls suggest either lower-than-expected development activity or the council's fee models are out of step with market conditions. Either signals weaker economic growth in the area.
findings.figures: Economic Regeneration and Planning variance £1.051m overspend 'largely attributable to a shortfall in Planning fee income'
findings.quote: The variance is largely attributable to a shortfall in Planning fee income, which continues to underperform against budgeted expectations.

findings.headline: One-off funding sources masking structural deficits; base cost pressures will hit 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that one-off funding sources (grants for pay awards, NI compensation, contingency draws) are 'merely defer most of the problem a year'. The excess unbudgeted base costs will 'impact directly and significantly on the base budget pressures for 2026/27'. This signals that the reported 2025/26 balance is not sustainable.
findings.matters: A council solving budget problems with one-off draws has not solved its structural issue. The £0.868m underspend is an artefact of timing, not genuine balance. This is a leading indicator of deficit spending ahead unless new savings are found.
findings.figures: Net underspend £0.868m at directorate level, but held for service overspends via contingency (£0.839m) and inflation (£3.571m) provisions
findings.quote: The one-off nature of the funding sources cannot be understated, the excess unbudgeted base costs will impact directly and significantly on the base budget pressures for 2026/27 and do not solve the inflationary pressures, merely defer most of the problem a year.

findings.headline: Equal pay liability review underway with high likelihood of requiring substantial new provision
findings.detail: The council is currently reviewing its equal pay position and reports 'there could highly likely be a need at some point to set aside a further substantial sum of money' to cover potential liabilities. Currently disclosed as contingent liability and existing provision in draft accounts. No quantified amount given, but the language suggests material exposure.
findings.matters: Equal pay provisions are a known liability across English local government. The council's language ('highly likely') suggests they expect charges ahead. The size is unknown but already earmarked contingency (£0.036m temporary funding) suggests this is not a small matter.
findings.figures: Contingency allocation includes £0.036m 'Temporary funding for Equal Pay Administrator'
findings.quote: There is also a significant risk emerging around equal pay liabilities – the authority (in line with other Councils) is currently reviewing its position and there could highly likely be a need at some point to set aside a further substantial sum of money to cover the potential liabilities

findings.headline: General Reserves already at absolute minimum despite bolstering over past two years
findings.detail: The S151 Officer explicitly reports that General Reserves are 'already at the absolute minimum of acceptability to the S.151 Officer, despite being increased over the past two years'. This statement during a year forecast to show underspend (due to contingency draw-downs) signals minimal headroom for 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.matters: Minimum reserves limit the council's ability to absorb income shocks, demand spikes, or failed savings. Combined with one-off mitigation throughout 2025/26, this leaves the council exposed going into 2026/27.
findings.figures: General Reserves at absolute minimum; contingency fund forecast balance only £0.839m remaining from £21.209m available
findings.quote: it has low General Reserves already at the absolute minimum of acceptability to the S.151 Officer, despite being increased over the past two years

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account projecting £6m overspend by year end, primarily from day-to-day repairs and voids, described as "unacceptable and unsustainable
findings.detail: The HRA is projecting a £6m overspend by year end, primarily in day-to-day repairs and void management costs. The council explicitly states this is 'unacceptable and unsustainable' and notes that if revenue cannot be contained, capital funded by revenue will have to be cut back significantly. This is a material constraint on the council's housing investment programme.
findings.matters: HRA overspends directly constrain capital investment in housing stock. A £6m shortfall suggests either structural under-budgeting of maintenance liabilities or rapidly changing repair costs. Either indicates housing condition risk.
findings.figures: £6m projected HRA overspend by year end; decrease from Q2 suggests some mitigation effect, but position remains 'unacceptable and unsustainable'
findings.quote: If this trend continues then end of year projected overspend is circa £6m, largely down to day-to-day repairs and voids. This remains a significant overspend, which is both unacceptable and unsustainable.

findings.headline: Social Services overspending £2.414m driven by commissioned care demand exceeding funding
findings.detail: Adult Services is experiencing significant overspends in commissioned care: Learning Disability £2.7m, Younger Adults £2.1m, and Older People £1.6m. These pressures, combined with unfunded pay and National Insurance costs, are being partially offset by staffing underspends in Child & Family Services, but the underlying demand pressure is material and recurring.
findings.matters: Social care demand pressures are growing faster than funding. The council cannot control these costs through savings plans and must absorb them from reserves or contingency. This is a leading indicator of structural budget stress.
findings.figures: Social Services total overspend £2.414m; Learning Disability £2.7m overspend, Younger Adults £2.1m, Older People £1.6m; pay and NI pressures £582k
findings.quote: We are experiencing pressures across our commissioned care services and currently expect overspends of £2.7m for Learning Disability Services, £2.1m for Younger Adults and £1.6m for Older People.

findings.headline: Savings delivery falling short by £1.7m against £13.974m target
findings.detail: The council is forecasting only 88% achievement of planned savings (£12.237m delivered against £13.974m target). The gap requires continued mitigation actions through the year and raises questions about the sustainability of the remaining budget balance into 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council unable to deliver its own savings plan signals either overly optimistic planning or operational challenges in service transformation. The shortfall is being masked by one-off contingency draws rather than structural cost reduction.
findings.figures: £13.974m target, £12.237m forecast delivery (£1.737m gap, 88% achievement rate)
findings.quote: against a savings target of £13.974m, £12.237m or some 88% is forecast to be achieved by the end of the year

findings.headline: Decarbonisation of the housing stock is assessed as unaffordable within the current HRA business plan.
findings.detail: The council states that the investment required to completely decarbonise council housing is unaffordable within the HRA business plan and will require additional investment and support from Welsh Government. This represents a separate unaffordable obligation in addition to WHQS 2023 compliance.
findings.matters: Unaffordable regulatory requirements represent future obligations the council cannot currently fund; this indicates high dependency on external grant support and creates risk if grant availability changes.
findings.figures: No specific figure quantified; noted as separate from £960m WHQS requirement
findings.quote: The investment required to completely decarbonise the Council's housing stock, however, is assessed as unaffordable within the HRA's business plan and will require additional investment and support from Welsh Government to achieve this aim.

findings.headline: The current year capital programme is already slipping due to design resource constraints, environmental requirements, and contractor negotiation delays.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 revised budget is £54m against an original £56m, with projected outturn of £51.3m and £2.7m slipping into 2026/27. Delays are attributed to specialist design resource availability, Natural Resource Wales marine nitrate requirements affecting More Homes projects, extended contract negotiations on high-value highrise work, and complex ecology issues on site requiring additional investigation and design.
findings.matters: Slippage in the current year indicates delivery challenges that could affect multi-year capital programme delivery; external dependencies (environmental regulators, planners, specialist resources) are emerging as constraints.
findings.figures: Original 2025/26 budget £56m; revised £54m; projected outturn £51.3m; £2.7m slippage
findings.quote: Slippage from 2025/26 into 2026/27 has occurred in some work areas due to the following issues; the need to secure specialist design resources, the impact from Natural Resource Wales instruction on marine nitrates affecting More Homes Projects, high-value highrise project requiring additional time for contract negotiations and complex projects requiring in-depth investigation and design leading to the schemes taking longer to reach the delivery stage.

findings.headline: The council is borrowing an additional £74m to fund the four-year capital programme, bringing total HRA debt to £189m.
findings.detail: The capital budget proposals require new HRA borrowing of £74m between 2026/27 and 2029/30. Total HRA borrowing is forecast to reach £189m by 31 March 2026. This additional borrowing is necessary to bridge the gap between the capital programme and available grants plus revenue contributions.
findings.matters: Increasing HRA debt and debt serviceability are key measures for lenders assessing financial sustainability; total debt levels and the rate of debt growth directly affect credit risk and the council's borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £74m new borrowing 2026/27-2029/30; £189m total HRA borrowing forecast at 31 March 2026; £268m total four-year capital programme
findings.quote: The funding of the attached capital budget proposals requires additional borrowing of £74m for the period between 2026/27 and 2029/30. Total forecast of outstanding HRA borrowing on 31 March 2026 is £189m.

findings.headline: Rent income came in lower than forecast, reducing revenue available for capital and intensifying pressure on repairs budgets.
findings.detail: The council states that rent-setting policy delivered lower income than forecast for 2025, increasing pressure on the revenue repairs budget. This is cited as a direct reason why the council cannot fund full WHQS 2023 compliance and is constraining the capital investment capacity available to the HRA.
findings.matters: Revenue shortfalls that reduce capital funding capacity indicate structural financial pressure on the HRA; lower-than-forecast income signals risk in rent projections and revenue sustainability.
findings.figures: Rent income forecast for 2025 was not achieved; amount not specified
findings.quote: This is in part due to the extent of the demands of Welsh Government's WHQS 2023, a legacy of the rent setting policy, which was lower than had been forecast for 2025, increasing demands on the revenue repairs' budget and limited grant support.

findings.headline: Welsh Housing Quality Standard 2023 requires £960m of investment over 10 years but the council has explicitly assessed this as unaffordable.
findings.detail: In September 2025, the council estimated the capital investment needed to fully meet WHQS 2023 at £960m over 10 years. The paper explicitly states this is 'unaffordable' and that 'available capital investment is insufficient', so the four-year programme is prioritised by contractual obligation and legacy repairs rather than full compliance.
findings.matters: A legally mandated standard that the council admits cannot be met within available resources represents a material financial and governance risk; lenders need to understand unaffordable long-term obligations and how they will be managed.
findings.figures: £960m required over 10 years; £268m capital investment budgeted over next 4 years
findings.quote: It is estimated the Council will require £960m to meet all aspects of the standard in the next 10 years. Because this is unaffordable and the available capital investment is insufficient, the programme presented in this report is prioritised based on the following

findings.headline: Pay award assumption assumes 2.5% annual increases for local government and teaching staff, but plan explicitly states higher awards could 'change significantly the projected deficit.'
findings.detail: The plan assumes 2.5% annual pay awards for both local government and teaching staff. However, paragraph 88 flags this as a high-risk assumption: "This has the potential to change significantly the projected deficit towards the end of the planning period." If actual pay awards exceed 2.5% (as occurred in 2022-23 when public sector awards ran 4-5%), the deficit projections would be materially worse with limited mid-plan correction options.
findings.matters: Pay is the council's largest cost base. A 1% variance against this 2.5% assumption costs roughly £7m-£8m annually across all pay budgets. Multi-year pay award inflation is a live risk in the UK public sector and this plan has minimal contingency.
findings.figures: Assumed pay inflation: 2.5% per annum for Local Government staff and teaching staff. No contingency provided for higher awards.
findings.quote: This has the potential to change significantly the projected deficit towards the end of the planning period.

findings.headline: Council faces £1.2m increase in Fire Authority levy over three years (from £600k to £1,800k), independently set by Fire Authority with no council control, described as 'obliged to fund.'
findings.detail: The council has no discretion over the Fire Authority levy; it is independently decided and the council is legally obliged to pay increases in full. Over the MTFP period, this levy rises from £600k (2027/28) to £1,800k (2029/30), a £1.2m cumulative increase. This is a known but uncontrollable cost escalation that erodes the council's savings programme.
findings.matters: A lender sees an uncontrollable cost that the council cannot negotiate, defer, or avoid. It reduces the council's flexibility to manage its own finances and pre-commits resources to a third party's spending decisions.
findings.quote: The Council is obliged to fund any increase in levies from the Fire Authority, the Corporate Joint Committee and Swansea Bay Port Health Authority.

findings.headline: Council's capital programme depends on capital receipts materializing; if receipts do not materialize, only alternatives are service cuts or additional borrowing.
findings.detail: The capital strategy explicitly assumes capital receipts will be achieved. Paragraph 36 states: "should such capital receipts not materialise the Council will have no option but to consider reductions in spend, seek alternative sources of funding or, as a last resort, consider additional borrowing which shall place a further burden on revenue finances." The council is betting on property sales and receipts in a soft property market, with no contingency other than more borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are unpredictable in the short term. If the council's property sales do not proceed as planned, it either cuts services immediately or increases external borrowing, both of which worsen financial resilience.
findings.figures: Capital programme includes Sustainable Communities for Learning £417m investment (£112m locally funded), Swansea Bay City Deal schemes, and others; exact capital receipts target not specified in the MTFP but is material to the plan's balance.
findings.quote: should such capital receipts not materialise the Council will have no option but to consider reductions in spend, seek alternative sources of funding or, as a last resort, consider additional borrowing which shall place a further burden on revenue finances.

findings.headline: Schools hold highest collective reserves of any local authority in Wales but council explicitly states this position is 'not sustainable' without additional Welsh Government funding.
findings.detail: Paragraph 84 states: "Our schools are in the privileged position of having the current highest collective reserves of any local authority in Wales." However, it immediately warns: "that position is not sustainable and it will provide a natural brake on the ability to expect schools to make further budget savings without wholescale redesign." Schools are expected to spend reserves in the short term but this is acknowledged as a temporary solution. The plan assumes only small schools savings requests for the MTFP period, but also notes: "the medium-term impact is that this will significantly impact Schools unless significant additional funding is forthcoming."
findings.matters: A lender understands that reserve-spending buys time, not solvency. Swansea's school sector is one spending shock away from forced service reductions, and the council acknowledges this will happen unless Welsh Government increases schools funding.
findings.figures: School reserves described as highest collective level in Wales. No specific figure given for schools reserves or the depletion timeline.
findings.quote: that position is not sustainable and it will provide a natural brake on the ability to expect further savings contributions. The clear aim is to support and protect schools in the short-term as much as possible, however the medium-term impact is that this will significantly impact Schools unless significant additional funding is forthcoming from the Welsh (and ultimately UK) Government.

findings.headline: Council locked in historic all-time low PWLB borrowing rates from 2021/22; borrowing costs forecast to rise significantly from 2029/30 onwards.
findings.detail: The council took advantage of all-time low PWLB rates in 2021/22 to borrow for capital schemes. The plan now forecasts that borrowing costs will show "a gradual increase from 2026/27 until 2029/30 when a significant increase in borrowing costs is expected." The council has £50m general borrowing and £25m Mumbles coastal defence borrowing already deferred. If interest rates remain elevated beyond 2029/30, revenue financing costs could exceed plan assumptions.
findings.matters: A council's borrowing costs are its largest fixed-term commitment. Rising rates from 2029/30 mean either higher revenue costs or deferred capital schemes. This constrains the council's financial flexibility precisely when the savings programme is most demanding.
findings.figures: £50m general deferred borrowing; £25m Mumbles CMRP coastal defence deferred borrowing; £22m Minimum Revenue Provision annually for debt repayment.
findings.quote: gradual increase from 2026/27 until 2029/30 when a significant increase in borrowing costs is expected to deliver the full externalisation of only the currently agreed deferred borrowing (£50m general and £25m Mumbles CMRP coastal defence scheme).

findings.headline: Unquantified equal pay liability explicitly identified as ongoing risk with no financial provision made.
findings.detail: The plan lists equal pay claims and review work as an ongoing, unresolved issue but makes no provision for costs. This is mentioned twice as a material risk. The S151 Officer acknowledges it could have future implications but has not modelled any cost impact, leaving the true financial position potentially materially understated.
findings.matters: Equal pay settlements can be large, back-dated, and move quickly. A council with unresolved equal pay risk has an unquantified contingent liability that could force emergency budget action.
findings.figures: None quantified in the plan.
findings.quote: Any ongoing implications that may arise from the equal pay claims and review work currently underway.

findings.headline: Escalating savings requirement depends entirely on unconfirmed 2% annual Welsh Government funding increases; if funding is flat (0%), council needs £29.6m additional savings over three years.
findings.detail: The plan balances only if AEF (Aggregate External Finance) grows 2% annually. The Welsh Government has confirmed funding only for 2026/27; no guidance given for future years. The plan explicitly states: if AEF turns out to be 0%, the additional savings needed would be £9.7m (2027/28), £19.6m (2028/29), and £29.6m (2029/30). At 4% growth, there would instead be a £31m surplus. This represents a £60m swing in the financial position based on a single assumption.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the balanced budget is robust or hangs on a funding guess. If settlements prove lower, the council faces immediate, mid-plan choices between uncontrolled borrowing or emergency service cuts.
findings.figures: Cumulative Savings Requirement: £8,309k (2027/28), £17,474k (2028/29), £18,271k (2029/30). If AEF 0%: additional savings needed £9,700k, £19,600k, £29,600k respectively. If AEF 4%: surplus available £10,000k, £20,000k, £31,000k.
findings.quote: The compounding effect of this key assumption is substantial over the life of the MTFP – the savings ask could be considerably higher if the actual increase is less than the range used as a planning assumption or considerably less if the settlements are more than assumed.

findings.headline: Finance costs rising by £813k due to increased borrowing for capital investment
findings.detail: Capital financing charges will increase by £813k in 2026/27 due to the council delivering its largest capital programme to date in response to WHQS requirements and More Homes Programme obligations. The council notes this increase was anticipated given the economic climate.
findings.matters: Rising capital finance costs indicate the council is borrowing heavily to meet statutory housing obligations; this increases fixed debt service costs and reduces flexibility if cost pressures return to HRA operations.
findings.figures: Finance costs increase £813k in 2026/27; capital programme £69.5m
findings.quote: Capital Financing Charges – These will increase in 2026/27 which was anticipated given the current economic climate and line with delivering our largest capital budget programme to date.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage from £56m to £54m with risk of further deterioration
findings.detail: The HRA's capital budget has been reduced from £56m to £54m due to natural slippage, with the possibility of additional slippage. This occurs whilst the council is planning its largest capital budget programme to date (£69.5m in 2026/27) and pursuing the More Homes Programme, suggesting delivery capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Repeated capital delivery slippage indicates project management or funding constraints; it delays asset maintenance and new affordable housing delivery, extending the HRA's exposure to further inflationary cost pressures.
findings.figures: Capital budget reduced from £56m to £54m; 2026/27 capital programme £69.5m; revenue contribution to capital £30.2m
findings.quote: Capital budgets have been reduced from £56m to £54m due to natural slippage with the possibility of this slippage increasing slightly

findings.headline: New statutory housing standards (WHQS 2023) explicitly stated as unaffordable without external subsidy
findings.detail: The Welsh Housing Quality Standard 2023 imposes new mandatory investment requirements with no additional external funding from Welsh Government. The council faces three competing statutory/policy priorities: maintaining existing stock condition, increasing affordable housing supply (to address homelessness crisis), and meeting WHQS 2023 compliance. The council explicitly states these cannot all be delivered.
findings.matters: A statutory obligation that the council explicitly says cannot be afforded creates covenant breach risk, suggests borrowing will be required for compliance, and flags delivery failure if rent income does not grow or if cost inflation continues.
findings.figures: WHQS 2023 requires significant extra investment; no funding gap quantified
findings.quote: Unless more income from rent can be achieved or there is significant funding from Welsh Government these requirements are unaffordable and cannot be delivered in full.

findings.headline: Largest investment programme (QED/Schools circa £400m) not fully approved; subject to Welsh Government review in 2027
findings.detail: The QED/Sustainable Communities for Learning programme represents the largest component of the capital programme. Welsh Government approval was only given 'in principle' for years 1-6 in August 2024, and the SOP is subject to preparation for the next WG review in 2027. Individual projects require further WG approval and business case development.
findings.matters: Funding uncertainty on the largest programme creates delivery risk. WG funding conditions could change, forcing scope reduction, deferral, or forcing the council to fund gaps from its own resources.
findings.figures: QED programme circa £400m overall; current profile £371.723m; WG approval 'in principle' only for years 1-6
findings.quote: Each of the investment priorities will be subject to detailed business case development and further WG approvals, together with separate reports to Cabinet for decision.

findings.headline: Capital receipts funding risk: only £6.485m planned from a £654m programme over six years
findings.detail: General fund capital receipts of just £6.485m are planned to fund 1% of the total six-year programme. The risk table identifies 'General fund capital receipts do not materialise at the level planned' as a key risk with impact of 'Funding shortfall', meaning any shortfall would require additional borrowing to fill the gap.
findings.matters: Low planned receipts means the programme is almost entirely dependent on external grants and borrowing. Any failure to realize planned asset sales will force additional unplanned borrowing or project deferral.
findings.figures: £6.485m capital receipts planned vs £653.952m total programme (0.99%)
findings.quote: General fund capital receipts do not materialise at the level planned | Funding shortfall

findings.headline: Revenue budget already under strain, limiting council's ability to absorb additional capital financing costs
findings.detail: The paper explicitly references an 'already challenging revenue budget scenario' and states that additional capital financing costs risk impacting this constrained revenue position. This suggests the council has limited headroom to absorb rising debt service costs from the £168m borrowing programme.
findings.matters: If revenue budgets cannot absorb rising debt service, the council will face service cuts or further borrowing, creating a vicious cycle. A lender needs to know whether debt service is sustainable from operating revenue.
findings.figures: No specific reserve figures, but programme assumes costs supportable from 'likely future revenue budgets affordably and sustainably'
findings.quote: any capital expenditure that leads to an overall net increase in borrowing costs brings with it the potential to impact on an already challenging revenue budget scenario going forward.

findings.headline: Capital governance weaknesses identified in WLGA peer review; new oversight board launching March 2026
findings.detail: The council's capital governance has come under external peer review by WLGA. Recommendations are being implemented during 2026/27, including launch of a new capital oversight board in March 2026. This indicates previously identified governance gaps in capital planning and delivery.
findings.matters: Weak capital governance historically correlates with cost overruns, poor project selection, and wasted capital investment. The requirement for remedial action signals prior control deficiencies.
findings.figures: New capital oversight board launching March 2026
findings.quote: The councils capital governance is currently under review following the WLGA Peer Review. Work will soon conclude on addressing the recommendation from the review to strengthen capital governance and capital planning. A new capital oversight board will be launched in March 2026

findings.headline: Unsupported borrowing requirement of £168.078m over six years with financing costs forecast to be materially higher than recent past
findings.detail: The capital programme of £653.952m requires £168.078m in unsupported borrowing. The paper explicitly forecasts that financing costs will be materially higher than previously because of higher gilt yields. This constrains the council's policy choices and limits capital capacity available for discretionary investment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt trajectory and the rising cost of debt service. Material increases in financing costs reduce the revenue available for service delivery and signal exposure to interest rate risk.
findings.figures: £168.078m unsupported borrowing requirement; £653.952m total programme; £654m with £50m headroom envelope
findings.quote: The costs of financing the same are forecast to be materially higher than the recent past noting the higher gilt yield environment, which in turn may limit the capital secured for any policy choice over the balance between revenue and capital priorities.

findings.headline: S151 Officer explicitly warns of revenue constraints limiting ability to service additional borrowing
findings.detail: The S151 Officer states that 'capital resource and importantly the revenue resources available to support any borrowing are both limited and finite' and references recent examples (Woking, Spelthorne) where 'overstretched, flawed capital programmes' resulted in S114 notices (formal financial failure declarations).
findings.matters: When a finance officer of a borrowing council explicitly warns of constrained revenue capacity, it signals genuine budget pressure and risk of future inability to service debt or fund services.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: it needs to be recognised that capital resource and importantly the revenue resources available to support any borrowing are both limited and finite. The robustness of the capital financing strategy is paramount in light of recent countless examples (Woking, Spelthorne) in local authorities in England where overstretched, flawed capital programmes has resulted in the issuance of a S.114 Notice

findings.headline: Major regeneration schemes anchored in City Deal extend financial obligations to 2032/33
findings.detail: The £1.3bn Swansea Bay City Deal regional programme runs until 2032/33, with major projects (Swansea Arena, Digital Village, UWTSD innovation facilities) already delivered and operational but generating ongoing revenue implications through management, maintenance and debt servicing.
findings.matters: Long-term regional commitments limit financial flexibility and create multi-decade revenue exposure even after capital delivery is complete; any deterioration in project performance affects revenue.
findings.figures: £1.3bn regional programme; individual project occupancy: 80% for Digital Village, ongoing visitor numbers for Arena
findings.quote: The Swansea Bay City Deal is a regional £1.3bn programme. The Swansea Bay City Deal Joint Committee remains in place until the full regional portfolio (nine projects) concludes and the benefit realisation period has concluded 2032/33

findings.headline: Governance review of capital delivery planned for 2026/27 following peer review
findings.detail: The council indicates that a peer review exercise has been completed and a governance review is planned for 2026/27. Currently, capital delivery is overseen by multiple boards (Regeneration, Housing Futures, Sustainable Communities for Learning) plus quarterly budget monitoring, contract procedure rules and financial procedure rules.
findings.matters: A governance review after external scrutiny suggests previous issues with capital management or project delivery; lenders should watch for findings and remediation.
findings.figures: Not applicable
findings.quote: there is a planned review of the corporate governance surrounding capital delivery in 2026/27 following a Peer Review exercise

findings.headline: Hundreds of millions in potential future capital requirements not yet funded or planned for
findings.detail: Beyond the approved capital programme, the council identifies 'potential substantial investments' for business continuity and statutory compliance (including sustainable learning communities and carbon zero obligations) that 'could lead to capital requirements in the hundreds of millions' but are 'definitively not afforded or factored into the medium or indeed longer term financial plans at this stage'.
findings.matters: Unfunded statutory compliance requirements create future budget shock and present a sustainability risk; they may force borrowing or service cuts within the medium-term planning horizon.
findings.figures: Hundreds of millions (unquantified)
findings.quote: Beyond these agreed projects there are also potential substantial investments that whilst only estimated at this stage, could lead to capital requirements in the hundreds of millions for not just Corporate Objectives but also to deliver business continuity or statutory compliance

findings.headline: Rising interest rates materially increasing cost of servicing capital programme
findings.detail: The council notes borrowing costs are 'forecast to be materially higher than the recent past noting the higher gilt yield environment'. The council previously took advantage of historically cheap PWLB rates (£90m in 2018/19 and £120m in 2021/22 at average 1.94%, described as 'cheapest borrowing ever undertaken by this Council'). Current rates are substantially higher, making future borrowing significantly more expensive.
findings.matters: Rising interest rates directly increase revenue costs of existing capital programme and make any new borrowing less affordable; this constrains both future capital investment and service spending.
findings.figures: Historical rates: 1.94% average (2021/22); current: 'materially higher' (not specified)
findings.quote: The costs of financing the same are forecast to be materially higher than the recent past noting the higher gilt yield environment, which in turn may limit the capital secured for any policy choice over the balance between revenue and capital priorities

findings.headline: Housing Quality Standard requires £960m investment but council can only fund prioritised portion
findings.detail: Welsh Housing Quality Standard 2023 compliance requires £960m over ten years to meet energy efficiency, carbon neutrality and other standards. The council admits this is 'unaffordable' and has created a prioritised programme (contractual obligations, maintenance, sustainability duties) that excludes full compliance. Decarbonisation work is only funded if Welsh Government provides specific grants.
findings.matters: A £960m unfunded capital need creates future budget pressure and regulatory risk; failure to meet housing standards could trigger intervention or enforcement action.
findings.figures: £960m required; only prioritised portion funded in current programme
findings.quote: In September 2025 an exercise was undertaken to understand the long-term capital investment needed to fully meet the standard. It is estimated the Council will require £960m to meet all aspects of the standard in the next 10 years. Because this is unaffordable and the available capital investment is insufficient, the programme presented in this report is prioritised

findings.headline: £168.078m unsupported borrowing requirement across 6-year capital programme
findings.detail: The council's capital programme totals £653.952m with £168.078m requiring unsupported borrowing (not covered by grant or receipts). This is described as 'significant' and requires substantial revenue funding to service the finance costs. The S151 Officer emphasises that revenue resources available to support borrowing are 'limited and finite'.
findings.matters: This scale of borrowing ties up a council's revenue budget for decades and limits flexibility to respond to service pressures or respond to new demands.
findings.figures: £653.952m total programme; £168.078m unsupported borrowing requirement
findings.quote: The updated total Capital programme which includes a 5 year forward expenditure programme plus current year of £653.952m identifying an unsupported borrowing requirement of £168.078m

findings.headline: UK Shared Prosperity Fund unwinding creates specific grant funding cliff
findings.detail: The S151 Officer warns: 'In particular in 2026/27 there will be a significant risk around the UK Shared Prosperity Fund as it begins to unwind. A further report to Cabinet in March is expected to accommodate the Local Growth Fund changes and targeted local additional support from the Council's own resources.' The SPF is being replaced with more capital-focused funding, requiring local top-up that does not fully replace what was lost.
findings.matters: Falling grant income forces budget reductions or reserves drawdown. SPF unwinding is not within the council's control.
findings.figures: £10m Economic Growth Fund being ring-fenced from contingency; SPF phasing out (specific amount not quantified in extract)
findings.quote: In particular in 2026/27 there will be a significant risk around the UK Shared Prosperity Fund as it begins to unwind... funding has reduced and will be more capital based, there will be a local top up to replace some of the funding but not all

findings.headline: Use of Capital Equalisation Reserve to balance revenue budget is non-standard and temporary
findings.detail: The S151 Officer flags a significant policy deviation: 'In 2025/26, for the first time, the revenue budget was predicated on drawing sums from the Capital Equalisation reserve solely for the purposes of balancing revenue pressures not to solely smooth the cost of capital financing in revenue. This is also built into the 2026/27 budget although there is an exit strategy built into the Medium Term Financial Plan. This is a deviation from previously agreed Council policy and is not considered by the S151 Officer to be strategic in deployment of reserves for their intended purposes.' They explicitly modify their Section 25 assurance on this point.
findings.matters: Using capital reserves for revenue is a sign of structural budget stress and reduces financial flexibility for capital investment.
findings.figures: Capital Equalisation Reserve drawn to support revenue (amount not specified in this extract)
